speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved:
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That this House condemn the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq and, encouraged by the unprecedented international consensus demanding the immediate and unconditional withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait and the full restoration of the legitimate government of Kuwait, affirm unequivocally its support for Canada's actions in the United Nations Security Council and its support for all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions adopted since August 2 and for the despatch of members of the Canadian Forces to take part in the multinational military effort in and around the Arabian Peninsula; and
That, upon adoption of this motion, the said motion shall be deemed referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last August 2 without provocation or warning, Iraq invaded Kuwait. Having overrun his smaller neighbour, Saddam Hussein claimed that Kuwaiti territory henceforth belonged to Iraq. Although he said that he had no further territorial ambitions, such assurances have been heard before. Fifty-two years ago this month, in Munich, the world learned a hard lesson about aggression and appeasement.
The world may have been surprised by the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait but no one was taken in by the justifications given for it. The invasion of Kuwait was seen for exactly what it was; a brutal aggression, a flagrant violation of international law and a challenge to the principles of the international order on which world peace depends. Iraq's aggression demonstrated how important that order is.
Tyranny is far from absent from international relations. Iraq's aggression also demonstrated how much the world has changed in recent times. Within hours of the invasion, condemnations of the Iraqi action were heard from Moscow and from Washington, from Cairo and Tel
Aviv, from Ottawa and Ankara and all outraged countries around the world.
In those early days of August we all rediscovered the value of an idea long buried under the snows of the Cold War. That idea, created out of the rubble of World War II, was one of peace through collective strength. That idea was that a civilized world community living by a common code of behaviour would have the will to stand up to tyranny and the means to respond to it. That idea was the United Nations.
The United Nations has emerged from this crisis in the gulf with new life bom at the end of the Cold War under the renewed determination on the part of many countries including, most importantly, former adversaries to make the idea of collective security work. In the seven weeks that have followed the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, we have seen the United Nations operate I think precisely as its founders would have envisaged and would have hoped. The Security Council has condemned the invasion. It has passed seven resolutions, the most recent following the armed entry by Iraqi soldiers into Canadian and other diplomatic residences in Kuwait and the detention by force of our representatives.

It has taken, partly at Canada's urging, a careful, determined and step-by-step approach under Chapter 7 of the Charter of the United Nations and has mandated a strict embargo of Iraq. There have been no vetoes cast, no superpower confrontations, no endless debates to mask impotence or disagreement. The Security Council has made it clear to Iraq that its annexation of Kuwait is unacceptable in the eyes of the entire world and that it will have to end. Last August, this was the position taken by all civilized nations, including Canada, and it is our position today.

The members of the United Nations have met Iraq's blatant disrespect for international law with firm and unflinching resolve. Saddam Hussein does not face a pile of toothless resolutions and pious hopes, as might have been the result in the not so distant past. Instead he faces the broadest global consensus of the modem era, perhaps of all time, expressed in the support for the embargo by over 150 countries. He sees before him Arabs and the Soviet Union joining with the United States and countries like Canada and Australia, all committed to the same fundamental and viable principle
September 24, 1990

that aggression must be resisted because when civilized nations fail to resist aggression, liberty will die.
Canada welcomes the crucial and skilled role played by President Bush of the United States in contributing immensely to building this important international consensus. The world is fortunate that the United States of America has both the political will and the military capacity to back up this leadership and to back it up quickly.
Some have suggested that the enforcement by armed force of international law and of the United Nations' resolutions is somehow contrary to the spirit of multilateralism and Canada's traditions. Nothing could be further from the truth. The willingness of the United Nations to authorize military means to enforce the resolutions it has passed may well presage an important new era for multilateralism, a goal for which generations of Canadians have worked.
Although the Iraqi leader has desperately tried to portray the conflict as one of the United States of America versus Iraq and the Arab world, he and his people must now know the fundamental truth that it is Saddam Hussein against the rest of the civilized world and, in that kind of conflict, Mr. Hussein will lose 10 times out of 10.
Saddam Hussein is facing the military forces of more than 25 nations. The determination of Egypt and Syria to play a significant role in the collective defence of Saudi Arabia was not only unusual and remarkable, but I think a most encouraging development not only for the present situation which we confront but future developments in the Middle East.
Throughout this crisis Canada has been active in a number of ways and the Secretary of State for External Affairs has played a vigorous and a most effective role in representing Canada throughout. We have focused our activities on three fronts, which the Secretary of State for External Affairs will elaborate on in much greater detail. First of all, diplomatic, in helping to orchestrate the United Nations embargo and in helping Canadians in the region. Second, economic, through respect of the embargo ourselves, not without cost. This has been a very costly. In fact I believe that the first effect of the biting of the embargo took place in Vancouver where 60,000 tonnes of Canadian wheat destined for Iraq were stopped in Vancouver harbour. This was a great hardship
Government Orders
for Canadian farmers but all Canadians have respected that embargo, and that too is most important.
And so economically, through respect of the embargo ourselves and through assistance to individuals and countries most severely harmed by Iraqi aggression; and militarily, through our despatch of men and women and ships and aircraft to the Gulf, we are doing our part.

As a member of the Security Council, we have been active in all its debates on this crisis. We have initiated some of the resolutions the Security Council has passed and we have participated in the drafting of others. We have argued for both firmness and balance.
And on behalf of all members of this House, I wish to offer our sincere congratulations to Ambassador Yves Fortier and his team for their outstanding work at the United Nations.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
When Saddam Hussein claimed that the embargo was starving Iraqi children, Canada took the lead in proposing that food be distributed under the supervision of an international body such as the International Red Cross, the approach that the United Nations adopted.
Our embassies have worked very hard with the Iraqi authorities to help stranded Canadians leave. And, we have kept open our embassy in Kuwait in the face of danger and of substantial hardship for our officials who have shown great courage. At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to digress, if I may, and offer, on behalf of all Members of this House, our sincere congratulations to our External Affairs staff in Baghdad and Kuwait which has represented the interests of Canadian citizens with such courage and dignity.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
On the economic front, we have worked for a strong embargo and supported the use of effective measures to ensure that it is not frustrated. We have scrupulously honoured that embargo ourselves. And this, Mr. Speaker, is an example of a measure that has proved costly to Canada. Canada has, also, supported the international efforts to respond to the human tragedies that the crisis has spawned.

Government Orders
In the way he has treated foreigners who had been living peacefully and productively in both Kuwait and Iraq. Saddam Hussein has shown the world the moral bankruptcy of his regime. With no concern for then-safety or survival, the Iraqi Government forced thousands of guest workers to flee through the deserts or Iraq to Jordan in the lethal heat of August. Canada was one of the first countries to commit funds to help international organizations deal with the complex problems of managing this vast outflow of displaced people, primarily into Jordan.
We subsequently announced a substantial expansion of that assistance, and approved as well a range of additional measures, altogether amounting to some $75 million. One of these measures will be the airlifting of displaced people to their home countries and providing special assistance to some of those countries least able to cope with the impact of thousands of returning citizens. Another such measure will be assistance to the countries of the region suffering serious side-effects from the crisis and from the sanctions against Iraq, especially Jordan, Turkey and Egypt.

And on the military front, we had little choice but to react quickly.
In August, when the Iraqis were massed on the border of Saudi Arabia, the situation demanded a prompt decision to stand up and be counted. Canada made that decision and we stood up and we have been counted.
Canada's response to the Gulf crisis was quick, clear, and unequivocal. When we dispatched three ships carrying almost 1,000 personnel, we decided at that time not to give their crews their specific mission tasking because we wanted to take into account the important evolution of developments internationally before doing so, given the normal time it would take for the Canadian ships to reach the Gulf. Subsequent UN resolutions, particularly resolution 665, confirmed, I believe, the appropriateness of this initial position and helped Canada define the
ships current mission, I believe, to the satisfaction of the military advisers of the Government of Canada.
On September 15, when our troops entered the operations zone, the Governor General signed the Order in Council placing them on active service for this mission. The Order in Council was tabled earlier this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence, consistent with parliamentary traditions. Members of this House have the opportunity to debate this matter fully before the ships arrive at station on October 2.
When it became clear 10 days ago that an additional contribution in the form of air support would be extremely helpful, not only for our own ships and the protection of our own personnel but for those of friendly nations as well, the Government of Canada decided to despatch a squadron of CF-18 fighter aircraft from Lahr, West Germany to the Gulf to protect Canadian lives and the Canadian operation. They will arrive in the area shortly and will be sustained by another 450 military personnel. We are also making Canadian civilian aircraft available to assist other countries in moving their forces to Saudi Arabia.
Some people have argued that Canada should not have sent planes and ships, and that taking on such a military role is incompatible with our role as a peacekeeper. Such arguments are based on a serious misreading of Canada's history. When called upon to play its part in collective efforts in the past to roll back aggression and to defend freedom, Canada has never shirked its responsibilities.
The sacrifices made by young Canadian men and women in two world wars are a proud and important part of our history as a nation. Those Canadians understood then, as we understand now, that the defence of Canada and of our ideals and values is not simply a case of protecting our own coasts, but also a case of preserving international order. It was precisely to defend those ideals and values that we contributed troops to NATO at great cost to Canadians and assigned them in Europe since 1951. It was to defend those precise ideals and values that over 25,000 Canadian troops fought in the United Nations engagement in Korea. And now our young men and women are called on to defend those ideals and values once again-this time in the Persian Gulf.



Our military response to Iraqi aggression is fully compatible with our traditions as international peacekeepers. Canada has been among the most active of all countries in multilateral peacekeeping efforts over the last forty-five years. Canadians have served in more than twenty peacekeeping operations, from the Congo to the Sinai, from Indochina to South Africa. And we are all proud of that tradition.

Our peacekeeping role-one in which we take great and I believe justifiable pride, which has distinguished Canada and where we have contributed enormously over decades to world peace-this peacekeeping role neither excludes us nor excuses us from the call to resist aggression. The roles are complementary as both serve the larger political purpose of preserving international order and both are very much in Canada's national interest.
There is no honour in claiming neutrality in the face of flagrant violations of international law. Canadians do not like the use of force and we have never in all our history chosen force as the preferred means of settling a dispute. But neither have we, at any time in our history, shrunk from using force when other means were exhausted, nor have we left the tough work to others in causes that we have supported. Canadians have never looked for a free ride and we are not going to start today.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Our contribution to the defence of freedom and our resistance of aggression constitutes chapters of sacrifice and glory in the history of this nation.
Throughout this crisis the protection of Canadians put in jeopardy by Saddam Hussein has been a major concern for the Government of Canada. We have evacuated as many Canadian citizens as possible and we have stayed in touch with those still there to offer whatever material, logistic, and moral support we can. I know that many Canadians are worried about members of their families still caught there and I know that all members of the House join me today in praying that those Canadians detained in Iraq and Kuwait against their will will not be harmed. Our hearts go out to these
Government Orders
families and I give them the assurance of all members of the House that we will continue to do all that we humanly can to make sure that we get their loved ones out and back to Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
We, and all other civilized nations in the world, are going to hold Saddam Hussein responsible for the well-being of our own citizens.
As I look back over the tumultuous events of the last 50 days or so, I see much of which Canadians can and will be proud: our sailors, and pilots, and soldiers who have gone courageously to the Gulf; our dock workers and specialists in Halifax who did months of work in a matter of weeks to get their ships ready; the members of the foreign services, to whom I referred a few moments ago, who have risked their own security and their lives and who have worked tirelessly to help stranded and detained Canadians; and the courage of Canadian families whose loved ones have been drawn into the vortex of this whirlwind inside Kuwait and Iraq.
I know that all Canadians do not want to see a war in the Gulf.

We all hope that the forces arrayed in the cause of peace will be sufficient to deter further aggression and to provide the leverage necessary to achieve a peaceful Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait. I give Canadians my assurance that we are doing everything we can, and will continue to do everything we can, to encourage a peaceful conclusion to this crisis.
But I give them my guarantee, as well, that we will not buy peace at the cost of dishonour to our history nor abdicate our share of the responsibility for preserving international order.

The many thousands of Canadians who have with great courage and great honour kept the peace in Africa and Asia and the Middle East and elsewhere around the world, understand why this must be so. The many thousands of Canadians-too many of whom lost then-lives at Vimy Ridge, Dieppe, on the beaches of Normandy, and the hills of Korea-would have wanted it no other way.

Hear, hear!

September 24, 1990
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I think I can say without any reservation on behalf of most Canadians that finally, at last, we have an opportunity in Parliament to begin to come to grips with one of the most serious and important issues facing the country in the last decade.
Many Canadians have been waiting for seven weeks for the opportunity in Parliament to express their concerns, to raise their questions, and, in fact, to find a way in which this country can play an effective role, a proper role, and an expanded role in this situation.
Let me first point out that our party, without any reservation, at all joins every other party, every other Canadian, and every civilized person in the world in condemning the aggression and invasion of Iraq into the state of Kuwait. We were all horrified at the brutality with which that aggression is taking place and the continuing impunity with which Mr. Hussein and the government of Iraq approaches its responsibilities under the United Nations and its obligations.

The Liberal Party of Canada unconditionally supports the broad international consensus condemning the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq. All member States of the United Nations must observe the provisions of the United Nations Charter and international law.
Taking a sovereign territory by force is an obvious failure to meet the obligations.

Also, I would like to join the Prime Minister in paying tribute to Canadian diplomats for their efforts to represent the interest of Canadians in the occupied state and the way in which the diplomats in the United Nations have carried out their functions with skill and the professionalism for which the foreign service has been known.
Also on behalf of my party, I would like to comment upon the uniqueness of this opportunity for an international response. We are so fortunate that events have come together to allow the United Nations once again to restore and play a role that had been denied it for so many years because of the cold war conflict and we can now hope that once again that the original charter seven responsibilities of collective security will be introduced.

We are encouraged by the role played by the United Nations in developing an effective international response to the Iraqi invasion. The UN Security Council has been particularly active, and the unanimity of its 15 members is both remarkable and welcome.

In saying those three things and in putting them on the record, I want to point to something the Prime Minister said in his remarks. I think his words were that this was a truly significant moment in world events and in the history of the country. If that is the case, if it was so significant, so crucial, and so vital, then why was Parliament kept in silence for seven weeks? Why were the people of Canada denied the opportunity to come together to address the issue? If the Prime Minister recognized how important and vital this matter was, why were the lights turned out in this building? That is a crucial question.
When it comes down to vital issues of international obligation, of war and peace, of sending Canadian troops overseas, to deny the opportunity for this Parliament to be heard or to represent the Canadian people, to have the question posed, is a dereliction of duty by the government, not by the troops, not by the forces but by the Government of Canada. That is really one of the serious problems this country faces. In fact, it was contributing to the malaise, the sense of great scepticism, almost cynicism, that the political system cannot even be employed at a time so crucial, to use the words of the Prime Minister, in our history.
I recall it was not that long ago when I was sitting at my cottage on Lake Winnipeg when all of a sudden I received a phone call from the Whip saying: "You have been called back to Parliament for a national emergency." "What was the national emergency?" I asked. "Has war been declared? Are the missiles coming?" He said: "No, 56 Tamils have arrived on the shores of Nova Scotia, and the government thinks that is so vital to the sanctity of this country that we must call Parliament back into session."
My goodness, 56 Thmils. Poor refugees. The homeless and the abandoned struggling ashore, and the full resources of the Government of Canada and Parliament are brought to bear for months of debate. By the way, the bill took almost a year to pass. What we see now, of
September 24, 1990

course, is that we have a backlog of 300,000 refugees and $285 million in expenditures. That is how much of an emergency it was.
I ask the Prime Minister: Does he not see the enormous irony that he could feel so compelled by the arrival of 56 refugees on the shores of Canada to say it is a national emergency and, at the same time, authorize 1,500 Canadian forces to a war zone, to an area of great critical risk, recognizing that Canada was undertaking historic obligations internationally but did not see fit to ask Canadians through their elected representatives what they thought?
The British Parliament managed that. Madam Thatcher has been criticized in many circles as not so close to being democratic. She managed to get Parliament back. What was interesting about that? What was interesting was that through the meeting of that Parliament, they were able to develop a consensus in a country. It was a bipartisan approach. It was an attempt to find an all-party agreement.
Mr. Kennock, on behalf of the Official Opposition there, spoke strongly in favour of the reaction. He raised some serious questions about the nature of the role in the United Nations and, I believe, helped in a very constructive way to formulate the proper approach for that country. I am not saying it is perfect, but it answered the debate. That is what this place is about.
This is not some kind of sausage machine where you simply turn out legislation and bills. Debate is essential to the spirit of democracy. When it is denied, democracy withers and dies. That is what we saw happening this summer.
Madam Speaker, I say through you to the Prime Minister that we are not here simply to rehash history. But, he has to realize that that was a mistake and that while in the resolution he is asking for unequivocal support, Canadians ask: "How can you be unequivocal when you have seen your own democratic system put on the shelf with the lights turned out? How can you be unequivocal in approving an action which is so demonstrably dangerous to the maintenance of our own democratic spirit in this country?"
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, public consultation should also be a key part of government policy when the government considers deploying military personnel. There must be a debate in this House to discuss all aspects of the matter and examine all problems, if the spirit of democracy is to mean anything at all in this country. This is essential.

But, we missed that opportunity.
Also, I want to raise an important question to the Prime Minister who is here, because he did not address it in his remarks. It is one I raise on behalf of many Canadians. I think it is important that he or his ministers address it as the debate ensues.
The resolutions passed by the United Nations deal with an economic embargo of Iraq. That is the chosen instrument by which the Security Council has made its decision of how to compel Iraq to withdraw from Kuwait. The endorsement of the use of military forces is to back up that embargo. There is no United Nations mandate covering the use of force in other circumstances. Those were unilateral decisions taken.
The key question that many Canadians are asking is are we going to adhere religiously to the UN resolutions dealing with the use of force or are we already beginning to extend out and push beyond the mandate of those resolutions? Clearly the sending of the maritime force was within the mandate of that resolution 6.65. No question. The sending of the CF-18s raises a somewhat different question because the military personnel themselves have said that in addition to providing air cover for the three ships going to the gulf, they are also going to be integrated into the other air defence wing and that there could be other uses in the deterrence of further attack.
Well, that is a very important distinction that has been made. It is not covered by UN resolution. I go back to the importance of the Prime Minister's words that this is an opportunity to build the United Nations, to give it a different kind of role, to enhance, enlarge and magnify its primary responsibility on decisions of conflict resolutions of collective security.
Therefore, we have to be absolutely careful that we do not contribute to any action that would subvert that role, change that role or question that role. If all of a sudden we are beginning to deploy troops and give them rules of

September 24, 1990
Government Orders
engagement or a mandate that extends beyond the clear definition provided by the UN, then we may also be in danger of undermining the opportunity of the UN to show it must be the place where decisions are made.
I noticed with interest the comments made by the Secretary of State in his visit to Washington-I believe it was on Friday-where he said we could envision the use of further troops, ground troops I presume or further aircraft troops. Would that be within the mandate of the UN? Perhaps this is the question that follows the one I just asked: Would it not be more important for Canada, occupying as it does a seat on the Security Council, beginning to ensure that those resolutions do cover the mandate, that there is not a question of unilateral decisions on war and peace, on deterrence or invasion or whatever other kind of military employment may be made?
That is why members of this party and others in the country who are knowledgeable and learned in this matter are saying that we as a country should be using our role, occupying that seat, to ensure that it is a United Nations mandate. This is not superpower bashing or anything else, but it is clear that there is a principle at stake. Do individual nations, whether they be large or small, have the right to decide when to use force for invasionary purposes? Whether it is in Grenada, El Salvador, Afghanistan or Iraq or if it is in response to something else, it should not be a unilateral decision. Surely the interest of countries like Canada, a middle power as it is often described or within that regime, which have represented so effectively since Suez the voice of countries that are not grand powers, says that we must establish a rule of law and a process to go along with it.
I agree with the Prime Minister that we honoured it to a point, but we are now talking about what happens from here on in. There is a mass of military build-up in Saudi Arabia-250,000 troops massing on the borders, massive tanks and everything else. There is a huge arsenal being built up. What is the purpose of that? Is it to deter further invasions of Saudi Arabia or others? Fine enough. But is it also, as has been mooted about, potentially to be used for a military solution to the problem? If the embargo does not work or people get impatient or it does not bite soon enough, will all of a sudden somebody else make a decision to use force to
compel Hussein to back off or to try to topple him as a tyrant? Who will make that decision? Will we be drawn in axiomatically as part of that decision because we have become part of the integrated command or that we are part of the Bahrain meetings or whatever other arrangements were being made.
I say to the Prime Minister very directly that it is a very important, crucial question. While Canadians have condemned the use of force by the Iraqis, they are not prepared to give a blank cheque for the use of force simply to get rid of them. They want it done with proper discussion and debate in this Parliament and in the United Nations. If it is to be used, then let it be used in that multilateral way, in that internationalist way which is very different from pure multilateralism. An internationalist way would build up the body of law, procedure and precedent to ensure that we have in place a clear commitment that unilateralism in the use of force should not be recognized. I in particular just raise raise the concern. The Prime Minister is certainly free to clear it up.
I do not have the actual copy of his statement, but he said that Canadians would not be afraid to use force if necessary, or words to that effect. Under what context? By whose decision? Our own or someone else's? By the United Nations? That is a very crucial issue.
I would hope that in the next day as this debate continues or however long we have that the government will answer that question. Is it prepared to make a commitment that there will not be further deployment of troops or the use of force without a clear, new mandate for the United Nations to do so. This means that we will clearly need to have a debate with the Security Council as to whether the sanctions have worked or not worked and then decide if in the interests of international peace and order that other options will have to be exercised. I certainly do not want that, Mr. Prime Minister. None of us in this House would contemplate it because we know what an enormous, incredible tragedy that would be.
As a result, we also want to pose some corollary questions to the Secretary of State arising out of the use of force. What initiatives, what actions are we taking as a member of the Security Council to seek a peaceful resolution? What kind of support? What is our state-
September 24, 1990

ment? For example, what is our position on the Soviet proposal for an international conference on the Middle East? What is the position of the government dealing with the proposed regional collective security proposal that the Americans have made, among others. These are crucial issues. What role?
I say this. It is important, and no one knows this better than the Secretary of State from his experience, that Canada play a positive role in making suggestions and making contributions rather than simply reacting to events, rather than simply responding to what takes place. Surely it is within our tradition.
I go back to the Pearson initiative of 1956, which was to find a way of resolving the conflict after an invasion.
I hope we can build upon that. I do not know if the Secretary of State is in the running for a Nobel Peace Prize. It certainly helped a past minister to become a Prime Minister. Who knows, lightening can strike twice.
The fact of the matter is that it is within the Canadian expectation. It has become part of our identity as Canadians. I know that there are a lot of cynics and sceptics around who say we make too much of our peacekeeping role. For many Canadians that is part of what we are. That is part of the basic traditions we have established as a country. We should not be simply engaged in the sabre rattling rhetoric, we should also be equally involved in the much more difficult, complex world of seeking some resolution.
God knows we have read the statements of Saddam Hussein and others. But there are initiatives being undertaken. Certain Arab nations are doing it. The Soviets are engaged in it. There are things under way.
Certainly it should be our role as Canadians to make a strong case at the United Nations to support those initiatives, just as we should also be raising serious questions about what happens after. The Middle East can never be the same. All the old rules are gone. Surely we are going to have to start asking ourselves some tough questions as a country about the kind of initiatives we wish to take.
As I understand it, one of the real reasons Saddam Hussein is able to build the kind of support he enjoys in certain parts of the Middle East is severe economic deprivation. The fact is that there has not been effective
Government Orders
economic planning or development in that part of the region for so long.
I think of the initiatives being taken now to raise funds.
I applaud the contribution of $75 million, but I see the kind of economic impact that will take place in countries like Jordan, Turkey and even in Third World countries because of the increase in oil prices. It is catastrophic and it is going to require a substantial reordering economically of the international order. I was waiting for the Group of Seven meeting in Washington this weekend to come up with some initial proposals. It said nothing about it as far as I could see. It ignored the problem in part. That is not good enough. As a member of the G-7 we should be making that case.
I would also like to raise a serious question with the Secretary of State or the government as to the stand we are going to take as a country on the arms embargo. One of the great tragedies of this whole event is the number of western countries, including many of our close allies, rapidly engaged in selling arms, chemical weapons and components of nuclear facilities to Iraq weeks before the invasion took place.
The Secretary of State will know that many times in the past I have been asking in the House for tougher rules both in our own country and internationally on the issue of the sale of arms and on the merchants of death, as they are commonly known in journalistic parlance. If there was ever a time for that case to be nailed tight and shut, it is now.
One of the real roles and opportunities for Canada in this crisis is to speak again with an unequivocal voice and indicate that there should be no more chemical weapons, components of nuclear weapons or arms sold to the likes of Saddam Hussein and other military dictatorships. That should be one of the ways in which we can say to the world: let's take this issue beyond just the simple call to arms and also begin asking what happens after. We should begin to say to people in the Middle East and elsewhere that we will no longer tolerate business as usual once this is over and that we need a different regime and a different set of rules for these kinds of countries.
All of them.

For all of
these countries, exactly. I agree. I say to my colleague who has had a long abiding interest in Middle East dramatics that that is true. Every country will have to examine its policies in this area to find peaceful resolu-

September 24, 1990
Government Orders
tions. I believe it would help now for Canada to be raising its voice, to begin suggesting how that could be done, and to be putting forward those kinds of proposals.
The Prime Minister's statement did not answer any of those questions for us. We do not have answers on what is the actual mandate of our troops. We do not have an answer on the question of whether we are prepared to go to war even though it is not mandated or sanctioned by the United Nations. Are we prepared to support offensive actions by our troops in the Middle East?
Under what conditions? Under whose decision? How will it be made? Under what kind of rules? Will Parliament be consulted? We would like to have answered now all those very serious questions which should have in fact been answered weeks ago.
We look forward very much to the opportunity to listen to members of the front-bench and other members of the government side trying to come to grips with the questions we have raised, because we believe those are the questions being raised by Canadians, not in any simplistic or naive way or not trying to get the Americans. It is simply that they are deeply concerned. They know that no greater decision of any government of any country can be made than that of dealing with war and peace. It is the ultimate question for all states to decide.
They want to be assured that those decisions will be made by all Canadians and that this forum, this Parliament of ours, will be honoured and consulted and used as a forum in which that decision, if it ever has to be made, will be made. More important even than that is the fact that we will do our best and our utmost to ensure that it is the United Nations as the repository for international order that becomes the place where decisions like that are taken, not in the capitals of individual states. That is crucial for us to make.
I say to members on the government side that when it comes to the resolution we certainly agree with the condemnation and certainly agree with and support the actions of the United Nations. However, we think the spirit of the resolution presented to us is not designed to
bring about a bipartisan approach which we can all support.
I wish it had been otherwise. I wish they had talked to us or asked us how we could have come together with a joint resolution of all three parties in this House. We could have had something that we could all support. We could have said that this was from where all Canadians speak, but it did not happen. In fact they included some words which they knew the opposition would have to take some quarrel with simply because of our concerns about both the past and present actions that have or have not been taken and the questions we have.
In that spirit I would like to present an amendment to the resolution, trying to work it into a more bipartisan approach. I expect my colleagues in the NDP will try the same because we are not approaching this matter in the way of scoring points or playing a parliamentary game. We realize just how deep and essential this is to the well-being of this country and the well-being of the world.
I would like if I might, Madam Speaker, to amend the motion this way:
That the motion be amended after the words "Canadian Forces" and read:
enforce these United Nations resolutions;
That this House censure the government for not recalling Parliament at the earliest opportunity to fulfil its legitimate function of consultation and debate as to what role Canada should play in the resolution of the present crisis; and
That upon adoption of this motion, the said motion shall be deemed referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade.
We believe this resolution or the amendment to it will go a long way in providing the kind of resolution that all Canadians can support of whatever party or whatever position so that we can stand united as a country on this very crucial matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The House has heard the terms of the motion. Resuming debate with the hon. member for Yukon.

Madam Speaker, I too rise to speak on motion No. 16 as presented by the government and to say that the New Democratic Party
September 24, 1990

unreservedly condemns the invasion of Kuwait. The New Democratic Party unconditionally asks for the withdrawal of Iraq from Kuwait, as this motion states.
As the previous speaker has said, I think we have to look at this matter in context of the base we are setting for the future and to discuss a number of issues relevant to it.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to see the House finally has a chance to discuss the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq which took place a little over seven weeks ago.
Let me make myself clear: the government has shown a flagrant disregard for parliamentary democracy and Canadian parliamentary tradition by failing to call back Parliament.
Madam Speaker, neither I nor my party can accept the use of Parliament for purely formal purposes. Canadians elect their representatives to think, to reflect, to criticize and even to advise, and that is what we intend to do.
Madam Speaker, first of all I want to say that my party and I have condemned the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq.
We think the international community must demonstrate its aversion to the ousting of the Kuwait government and its citizens.
We condemn the violations of the Vienna Convention on the rights of diplomats.
We demand the unconditional withdrawal of Iraqi troops from Kuwait.
We firmly support the five resolutions of the UN Security Council adopted on August 2, 1990, including Resolution 665.
We must do everything in our power to make the economic blockade a success.

We support a multinational force in the gulf to enforce United Nations resolution No. 665. We support every effort to ensure that the economic embargo is successful and that we arrive at a peaceful solution of this crisis.
I believe the United Nations is clearly our best mechanism for resolving this crisis. I want to give three
Government Orders
main reasons for this. First of all, the cold war is over and the United States and the U.S.S.R. have both condemned the invasion of Iraq. Second, most of the Arab world has condemned the invasion of Iraq. The United Nations Security Council has been unanimous in its position against the Iraqi invasion.
However, I would suggest that the Canadian government has made a fundamental error in the precipitous actions that it took that were not simply related to the embargo as approved by the United Nations.
I also believe the government has made a fundamental error in deciding to follow the lead of the United States instead of helping to lead in the United Nations.
Hear, hear.

This is the first post cold war crisis where the international community has been put to the test about how it might undertake multilateral actions in a consistent way, consistent with the United Nations charter and the precepts of common security.
As we have so often said in this party, our security cannot be kept through supporting the insecurity of others. That is why we see the United Nations having a role to ensure that there is common security, common actions, multilateral actions under the direction of the United Nations.
United Nations resolution 665 was passed on August 25, some 15 days after the government sent our Armed Forces to the gulf and 19 days after the Prime Minister had met with the President of the United States.
This government is losing an opportunity to live up to the intention of the San Francisco Conference of 1945 to function effectively when major powers are in agreement. I would remind you, Madam Speaker, that in this case major powers are in agreement. It is unfortunate in our view that the President of the United States decided to take things beyond the international consensus and has cast aside the United Nations. It is also unfortunate that the Prime Minister reacted too quickly to this President's demands.
In our view not only did the Prime Minister of Canada react inappropriately, but by following the U.S. plan this government has given Saddam Hussein an easy villain for his propaganda.

Government Orders
It is for this reason-and I agree with the speaker from the Liberal Party-that we would have wanted to see a resolution that brought together the views, the horror that all Canadians share about the actions of Saddam Hussein in invading another country, but would also allow us to have a debate in which we could look at the way in which it was done.
In his opening remarks the Prime Minister said something to the effect that Canada would stand up and be counted, that we would do our duty, that this was historic, this was significant. I agree that this is an historic and significant act that the Prime Minister has taken unilaterally without consulting this House, but there are ways to stand up and be counted. Why should we accept that the only way is the way that the Prime Minister has taken and that is to send three ships and now further to that CF-18s?
Surely there is another way. Could we not sit down and use our seat on the UN Security Council, for which we fought very hard, in a way which will provide the basis and the foundation for the United Nations assuming a role in this conflict, as in others, that will provide an agenda for peace and for a peaceful resolution.
I would have to say that this government has tended to use the United Nations as it has this Parliament, for approval after the fact. This is a bad strategy for Canada and, in my view, it is a bad strategy for world diplomacy. This resolution uses the United Nations as a rubber stamp. It diminishes its potential and it diminishes the role that Canada could be playing now that we are on the Security Council.
It is clear that independent, thought-provoking policy is not a priority of this government. This is a government that first of all joins the Organization of American States and its first action is to support the U.S. invasion of Panama. Finally, we win a seat on the Security Council and the first action in a major way that we take is to support the United States actions which circumvented unilaterally a United Nations decision.
Let us review the actions of the Canadian government before the crisis began. Three Canadian vessels were dispatched to the Gulf on August 10. There was no parliamentary approval and no parliamentary debate. In fact, the armed forces were not put on active duty
because to do so would have meant recalling Parliament. Ironically, our ships even had to slow down in order to avoid active duty status. Our CF-18s are on order to be dispatched but their mission is totally unclear. No other alternatives for a Canadian contribution to a multilateral effort appear to have been considered.
Now there is some confusion. There were no clear orders, no clearly defined role for our armed forces and many questions still remain that must be answered by this government. First of all, on what basis was it decided to send three naval ships? Second, what exactly did the U.S. President request of our Prime Minister? What did the Prime Minister promise to the United States President in terms of our action in the Middle East? This is not clear in the Prime Minister's statement today. Has the Prime Minister ultimately committed us to the use of ground troops? That was not clear in the Prime Minister's statement today. What is the military objective of our naval ships? What is the military objective of the CF-18s? I suppose the biggest question of all is: who is giving the orders? What is Canada prepared to do? We have seen what is happening, we have seen increasing support for Saddam Hussein in the Middle East, we see the possibility of a conflict between the United States and Arabs, not just Saddam Hussein. What will Canada's role be? Are we proposing an offensive role, a defensive role, or standing on the sidelines? It has never been made clear; it was not clear, even in the briefing given by the head of the armed forces and by the Prime Minister last week.
I believe that my party and I would have acted differently if we had had the opportunity. First of all, we would have held a full parliamentary debate-
Hear, hear!

-because we believe that an issue as important as this, an issue that could basically come to the question,"Will Canada go to war?", we need to hear everyone's views, everyone's solution, not in a partisan way but in a way to ensure that Canada, as a middle power, acts as a force for peace and uses its resources in a way to ensures that.
The Prime Minister referred to our role in peacekeeping and said that that was not undermined by the actions that he and his government took. It seems to me that if we had not been so precipitous in doing what we did, we
September 24, 1990

might have found a role that is much more in keeping with the traditions of Canada, that is peacekeeping, its role as a voice of reason and diplomacy. As we know, this was not done and Canada's troops are now in the Middle East. The question is, what do we do now? How do we maintain Canada's international reputation as a peacekeeper and how do we demonstrate that we are prepared to work with the United Nations, not simply follow one other nation's decision-making?
Madam Speaker, I propose that Canada adopt the following policies: given our limited military resources in the Persian Gulf, Canada should be poised to take future peacekeeping roles. In the meantime I recommend, as my colleague did earlier today during the Question Period, that our troops stay in the Gulf of Amman as was their original order and that Canada begin to position itself as a voice of reason and calm in the midst of high tension. I would add that if our troops were to remain in the Gulf of Amman, we could then assist in implementing Motion 665 of the United Nations regarding the blockade.
Second, I would propose that we must increase our efforts to help refugees from this area and use our seat on the United Nations Security Council to put increasing pressure on Saddam Hussein. Canadians must be wondering what we have done since we got that seat on the Security Council. All that most of us can see that Canada has done is simply to follow the United States before it has even made any kind of plan, proposed anything that the UN could become involved in, in a substantive way.
We would also work for a political solution; this is not just something that requires a military solution. We recommend that we should be attempting to revive the military staff committee of the United Nations which provides for the co-ordination of international military efforts, in order to maintain international peace and security. Surely this crisis in Iraq and Kuwait demonstrates the importance of having the United Nations mobilized so that it can deal with these issues, not after they have occurred but have a policy developed to deal with them before they occur. I would suggest that the Canadian government has a role to play and we should use our seat on the United Nations Security Council to make sure that the United Nations is in a position to use its authority in a useful and a positive way.
Government Orders
We cannot see this situation simply in the context of the invasion of Kuwait, although it is obviously the most serious issue at this point, we also must look and work for a long-term approach to the situation in the Middle East in general. My colleague, the hon. member from the Liberal Party, also mentioned arms shipments to Iraq. We simply are now reaping what many have predicted, including many in this party and myself, that to continue to sell arms to the Middle East wdl simply lead to very serious consequences and we see the consequences now. We must have an arms embargo in the Middle East.
Hear, hear.

I would add, Madam Speaker, that this country cannot see itself exempt from that. We know that we have participated in that and we have to take our own responsibility and not just point the finger at other countries. We also have to work to end the use of nuclear and chemical weapons.
Third, we must promote an international conference to resolve the longstanding Palestinian question. Let us not forget that Canada's longstanding and traditional role in international relations has been to provide diplomatic means as well as a force for peace in times of conflict. By participating in the present non-United Nations force, Canada may eliminate the possibility of playing a peacekeeping role in the future. There is a better way, and I say today that we must begin that task.
I would like to make a couple of other points and take a bit of time to send my prayers and those of my party to the Canadians still trapped inside Iraq and Kuwait. I also want to commend the embassy staff in those two countries for the hard work which they did under very, very stressful conditions. I myself had an opportunity to speak on a couple of occasions to those staff in Iraq specifically and I understand how very, very difficult and in a very fine way they did their job.
I also would like to extend my admiration and prayers to the Canadian men and women who have been sent to the Gulf. They are courageous Canadians who have already made many sacrifices so that we may live in a peaceful world. Let us all hope that none of them will have to make the ultimate sacrifice. Let us all today take

Government Orders
the responsibility which ensures that we, as politicians, will act in a responsible way to ensure that they do not.
Madam Speaker, there are three other short points I would like to make because I would like to propose an amendment to the government's motion. As we know, Iraq was our largest customer for Canadian wheat, and I would ask that the government adequately compensate Canadian farmers who are harmed by the Iraqi wheat embargo because it is very important to have a united front on this very serious issue.
I have said that we support unreservedly the first part of Motion No. 16 put forward by the government. We too condemn the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq. We too demand the immediate and unconditional withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait and the full restoration of legitimate government in Kuwait. But I would have to say that what has been added to this, that we simply rubber stamp the actions of this government is not acceptable. I take great offence that the government has put forward a motion which they know will not get unanimous consent because they simply have put in that section to rubber stamp their actions rather than to condemn the government. It is for these reasons that we cannot support the resolution as it stands before the House.
This government is using the United Nations, as it does its own Parliament, for approval after the fact.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the member for Burnaby-Kingsway:
That the motion be amended by adding the following after the
word "resolutions"
'And further, that Canada work at the Security Council to seek assurances that no country will undertake offensive military operations against Iraq unless they are under UN command and explicitly authorized by the Security Council."
