speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the decision was taken to send Canadian forces to join other nations in the gulf, there was an undertaking to initiate a discussion in
Government Orders
Parliament at the first appropriate occasion. The House resumed sitting today and this resolution has been introduced immediately.
If I may, I will deal for a moment with some of the matters raised by my colleagues on the other side. No opportunity has been denied parliamentarians to be heard on this issue. That opportunity is being exercised now. That is perfectly in accordance with the traditions and the practices of this Parliament in all situations that bear any resemblance to what we are dealing with now.
What departs from the tradition, if I may say so, is the attempt by my friend, the hon member for Winnipeg South Centre, to make this, not a debate about a question of great importance, but simply a partisan exchange, which he has done with his amendment. Naturally, I wanted to indicate on behalf of the government that we do not intend to support that amendment which would have that trivializing affect upon a debate which is very, very important.
The value of a debate is to know the views of other parties and other members in the House. The other parties who have spoken today will be judged on the basis of the matters they have brought forward.
My colleague from Winnipeg did raise some questions of importance and substance and I hope to deal with them later on. I always thought he wanted to be the external affairs critic and, for a while today, I thought he wanted to be the House Leader of the Liberal Party because most of his arguments were procedural, but some were not and I will deal with those later.
With regard to the Leader of the New Democratic Party, if I understood her correctly, one proposal she put forward was that the decision that was taken as to the deployment of our ships in the gulf, a decision taken by the Chief of the Defence Staff, should be changed by her critic on external affairs. I am not sure that the rest of the country is ready to have the judgment of the Chief of the Defence Staff substituted by the Member of Parliament for Burnaby-Kingsway. Certainly, we are not.
I was interested in her suggestion as to the amendment that she introduced. Since she took exception to the following language in the resolution now before the House-the affirmation of "support for Canada's actions in the United Nations Security Council and its support for all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions adopted since August 2-am I to understand that

Government Orders
the New Democratic Party opposes Canada's actions in the United Nations Security Council? Am I to understand that the New Democratic Party opposes support for all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions adopted since August 2? That would be a bizarre position.

On August 2, Madam Speaker, Iraq launched a general attack and invaded the sovereign state of Kuwait. This was an obvious breach of the most elementary principles of international law. It was an invasion made without provocation and in violation of the commitment made by Iraq as member of the United Nations to seek a peaceful settlement to disputes.
Even though the concentration of troops which preceded the violation of Kuwait's sovereignty did not go unnoticed, the rest of the world was shaken by the fact that Iraq should have so readily resorted to force.
Only a few days before the invasion Saddam Hussein had promised President Mubarak that Kuwait would not be invaded. The small country was quickly occupied and its government was replaced by a puppet regime whose nature was obvious. Realizing that the international community would not recognize this puppet administration, on August 8 the Iraqi quite simply decided to swallow Kuwait and announced that henceforth this country would be their southern provinces. All these measures violated international law and made people fear that the agression might well extend to Saudi Arabia.
Since then Iraq has increased its military presence and imposed strict occupation rules on the resisting population. It is now plundering public and private Kuwaitian assets.
Hundreds of thousands of foreign workers fled Kuwait and neighbouring countries, particularly Jordania, have to face the consequences: hordes of fleeing and penniless workers, economic upheaval and increased tensions.
Canada reacted by asking immedialtely that collective measures be taken to condemn and stop the aggression. On September 4 Canada officially suspended all commercial trade with Iraq and occupied Kuwait, froze the
assets of both governments and cancelled special provisions concerning trade promotion with the Iraqi and other commercial agreements.

When Iraq acted against Kuwait its aggression had to be stopped in its tracks to give time for the machinery of the international community to get to work. Iraq's clear ambitions against Saudi sovereignty and the threat of further direct action against it required an unequivocal demonstration of support for Saudi Arabia and for the gulf states. That immediate reaction allowed the United Nations to mount a response of unprecedented unanimity and effectiveness.
There have been questions raised about the United Nations' mandate, serious questions raised by my colleague from Winnipeg, and I assure him and the House that the Government of Canada has worked very hard within the United Nations to ensure that there will be full respect for the mandate of the United Nations.
We have encouraged our close allies, we have encouraged others, and we have used our influence and our position on the Security Council to ensure that the action that proceeds is action that is within the mandate of the United Nations and, indeed, that the mandate given by the United Nations expands to take account of the circumstances as they develop in the region. We are working very hard to have United Nations' auspices respected.
The member posed a question as to comments I made in answer to reporters in Washington on Friday. I was asked whether we had ruled out other actions that we might take. We have not ruled them out. We intend to take them in the context of the United Nations. We intend to take them in the spirit in which we have acted to this point, if we have to take them.
Remember what we are dealing with here. We are dealing with a situation in which world pressure has to be mounted and has to be maintained if there is any hope for diplomacy to work. That means that countries like ours, which have a range of measures which we might apply, have to be in a position to apply them as circumstances warrant. In our view, in the Canadian tradition, in the tradition of our actions in this crisis, we will be
September 24, 1990

acting within the context of the United Nations and encouraging others to respect the mandate of that organization.
But let me make this point. One cannot always wait for deliberative bodies to deliberate and to decide. Saddam Hussein did not wait. I was quite surprised by the suggestion of the Leader of the New Democratic Party, if I understood her correctly, that somehow Canada moved too quickly. Does she believe that Egypt moved too quickly, because it was at the same pace as Canada? Does she believe that Europe moved too quickly, because it was at the same pace as Canada? Does she believe that the Soviet Union moved too quickly, because it was the same pace as Canada? Does she believe that there should not-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No Soviet troops. There are Soviet ships and there has been Soviet action very actively on the Security Council. The point is that we cannot always expect events in the world to await the decisions of deliberative bodies. We can do what we can to ensure that those bodies move very quickly. I ask some questions. Perhaps there is a new position being put forward by the member for York Centre different from that put forward by his colleague from Winnipeg.
Let me take the proposal as I understand it by the member for Yukon, which was that Canada should have waited before signalling our willingness to send troops, before acting to freeze Kuwaiti assets in Canada so they could not be taken advantage of by Iraq.
She never mentioned it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not want to misinterpret her. Let me just stick to the issue of troops. If she was saying-and her critic is nodding his head affirmatively- that the position of Canada should have been that we should have waited until there had been UN action before we signalled our intention to join other countries in the Gulf, then I think that that raises some other questions.
One question it raises is: how long would she have had Canada wait? A second question it raises is: what does she think would have happened while Canada was waiting? What would have happened while Egypt was waiting? What would have happened while Europe was waiting? Does she believe that Saddam Hussein would have waited? Those are not rhetorical questions offered
Government Orders
in debate. Those are questions that have to be faced by serious parliamentarians recognizing that Canada's position here is not simply a position of passing resolutions but is a position of exercising our influence by the deployment of all of our resources, humanitarian resources, military resources and diplomatic resources.
There is no doubt at all that our ability, Canada's and that of other countries, to provide some room for the United Nations to work, our ability to stop Saddam Hussein in Kuwait and dissuade him from going on into Saudi Arabia depended upon the fact that there was a clear response on the part of a range of countries that further aggression by Saddam Hussein would not be accepted by the world.
The United Nations Security Council could not meet that quickly to deliver that message, but the message had to be delivered. I have no apologies for Canada being part of sending a signal that stopped Saddam Hussein and created an opportunity for diplomacy and the United Nations Security Council to work.
To come back to the central point, I assure the House that we have acted consistently to strengthen the role of the United Nations in this crisis, and we intend to do that. Canada's immediate and timely response, including the commitment to send our forces, contributed to stopping Iraq from more aggression. At the same time that we sent that signal we were playing a very active role in developing Security Council positions. The spectacular and historic success of the United Nations system in the succeeding weeks vindicated our faith in the ability of the world body to follow through with concerted measures against the Iraqi Government's actions and with policies consistent with Canadian values and precedents in foreign policy.
Resolution 661 passed on August 6 by the Security Council was key to that definition because it set out the sanctions which were to be imposed on Iraq. The intention of that measure was to end trade with Iraq. All ordinary commercial operations were to stop immediately. Critical for Canadians and indeed for all countries with nationals who now fall under the control of the Iraqis was resolution 664, which was passed a brief 12 days later on August 18. Saddam Hussein detained all males over the age of 18 from a group of countries, mainly western countries, which included Canada. Working women from black-listed countries were as well refused the right to leave freely.

Government Orders
The forces in the Gulf were given United Nations authority to use necessary force to halt maritime shipping and inspect cargoes to ensure that sanctions were being respected. Resolution 665 was passed on August 25 with two abstentions and was crucial to giving United Nations framework for the activities of naval forces in the area, including our own. In response to the manipulation of the food issue by Saddam Hussein, the Security Council had to define the precise conditions under which food could be sent to civilians in distress in Iraq and occupied Kuwait.
Resolution 666 of September 13 addressed the question firmly and unambiguously; if United Nations and some appropriate agency had to accompany any delivery to ensure distribution to the civilian population. Further measures are in preparation. The sanctions must be continually defined and tightened. They must be policed. My colleague from Windsor, who has worked with me on South African matters, knows how important it is to police embargoes and police sanctions that are in place. That has to happen here. A further resolution concerning an air embargo will be presented at the Security Council meeting tomorrow, an extraordinary meeting, at the level of foreign ministers, dedicated, among other things, to demonstrate the very high priority that all of the world attaches to this response.
If Iraq's attack was an extraordinary violation of international law, so was the world's response an extraordinary example of common purpose. The whole of the international community joined in condemnation of Iraq. The ships in the gulf are from Britain, France, the United States, the Soviet Union, Canada, Australia and Argentina. The troops on the ground are from some of these countries, plus Egypt, Syria, Morocco and Bangladesh. With remarkable courage, the majority of the Arab world has demanded that Iraq leave Kuwait. This is not east against west nor rich against poor nor Arab against non-Arab. This is the world coming together to stop aggression. Naturally, Canada has played its full role. We are advocates of international order. We seek to defend it when it is broken and we seek to extend international order when we can. Ironically, this aggression by Iraq may have created conditions where common action by the world may become more the rule and less the
exception. Certainly, it is Canada's intention to seek to extend this new consensus in the United Nations.
Questions were raised about arm's embargoes. There is no question that is a very important matter now, thrown into relief by the sources of weapons involved in this conflict. Canada's record, as a matter of fact, is a good record with regard to our own policies but other countries in the world are not so good. There is no point our being effective unless others are. There is an opportunity now for us, not by showing the way. You do not accomplish things necessarily by showing the way. You accomplish things by sitting down with others and moving them forward with you.
We have had some experience in moral leadership. Moral leadership is fine, Madam Speaker. Moral leadership is quite important. Moral leadership is particularly important for celebrating empty victories. But if you are interested in making some significant changes in international events, you have to combine moral leadership with a very sharp sense of what can be accomplished and that is what we have been doing here. I believe, and it will be Canada's intention in the Security Council and elsewhere, that it is now going to be possible for us to have a more secure and comprehensive regime with regard to arms exports than has been the case in the past and it may indeed provide momentum for the discussions on chemical weapons.
Again, we have some experience here. Canada's reputation, Canada's diligence on these issues, has been successful in extending the arms control embargo as it has applied in the past to South Africa. I think in these new circumstances it will be possible for us to use that same commitment and leadership and skill to advance the possibility of arms embargoes to help prevent future crises of this kind.
I was asked if we are examining options, I believe it was the question, that would lead Iraq to withdraw and certainly we are. May I make three points about that. As we undertake that, we want to be careful not to complicate the resolution of this issue by drawing in other questions which have on their own proved extraordinarily difficult to resolve. I know the position that is being put forward by Saddam Hussein with regard to the inter-relation of all of the issues in that region. I think that we are justified in seeking to resolve this particular aggression now. I take the hon. member's point that the
September 24, 1990

region has changed irreversibly and very substantially. The question for us to face is how do we respond to those changes and do we put at risk the possibility of moving Saddam Hussein back by bringing in other issues which, while they have to be resolved, might not best be resolved in this circumstance.
Second, we are naturally going to be consulting closely with the Government of Kuwait with respect to any matters that might affect the nation, the state or the sovereignty of Kuwait.
Third, our authorities are under instruction as those of others in the world are to seek urgently imaginative options that might make a difference in this particular crisis.
The hon. member raised a question generally. I have tried to reply to him to indicate that we are looking very actively with as much imagination as we can to ways in which Canada might either find options that would work or advance them.
A point has to be underlined. I note that I am at the end of my time. This conflict is very dangerous to the world. Its ramifications will dominate global policy making for years to come. The challenge will be to maintain unwavering and consistent pressure to give diplomatic avenues a chance to succeed, but there must be a recognition on the part of the House and on the part of the country at large that there is no certainty that this issue will be resolved quickly.
We are in a very dangerous time in the world. We have an obligation as a country which has earned its credentials as a peacekeeper, diplomatically and militarily. We are under an obligation to deploy all our resources in ways that are consistent with our traditions and interests. That is what we have been seeking to do.
Yes, we have been innovative. Mr. Pearson was innovative when he stood against people who criticized the idea of using military forces in any peacekeeping role at all. We are prepared to be innovative in these circumstances, but we believe there is a requirement upon Canada to deploy all our resources-military, diplomatic and humanitarian-so that we can contribute in the best Canadian tradition to a resolution of a crisis that is as serious as anything we have known in decades.
Government Orders

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments on the amendment to the amendment as moved by the previous speaker.

Madam Speaker, I had an opportunity to speak and I will leave it to other members, but there was one question that I will just put to the government side. The Secretary of State was good enough to answer several questions, but he missed this one and it is crucial.
As we now stand in the present situation, we are looking at very long, protracted sanctions in the gulf which could take months. We are looking at a very major military build-up that is taking place in Saudi Arabia with the various multinational forces, and we are looking at a potential military option.
We would like to get some assurance specifically from the government that we will not engage in any offensive action in this region unless there is a consent of Parliament and a mandate from the United Nations. Can the minister give us that assurance?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are anticipating no offensive action. We cannot anticipate what Saddam Hussein might do. We cannot anticipate threats that might arise to Canadians, and I think the hon. member would want us to respond to those threats as appropriate.
I do not contemplate circumstances under which our anticipation would change. I give you my assurance that if the House is sitting, if it is not a weekend, if it is a week day, we would come to Parliament in the very unlikely event that what we anticipate changes. If not, that I or others would seek to consult with the spokesmen of other parties.
We are also urging, I should add, other countries to work within and to stay within the United Nations mandate. Part of our success in that will depend upon the United Nations mandate continuing to be large enough and contemporary enough to changing situations in the gulf that the temptation for other countries to operate outside it would be reduced.

Madam Speaker, I would like to deal with the latter point made by the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs. Of course the current mandate given by the Security Council is very specific with respect to the use of force in that area, and that is the mandate under resolution 665. It is strictly for purposes of enforcing

September 24, 1990
Government Orders
resolution 661. There is no other security council mandate at this point, as the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs is well aware.
I want to point out to the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs that in fact-and I am sure it was unintentional on his part-he did unfortunately misrepresent the position taken by the leader of my party during her very eloquent contribution to this debate. The leader of my party made it very clear that the portion of the main motion to which we take exception are the words after "August 2"; in other words, the words dealing with "the despatch of members of the Canadian Forces to take part in the multinational military effort".
We have condemned the invasion. We have urged Iraq to recognize its responsibility to withdraw unconditionally from Kuwait. We have indeed supported Canada's role in the Security Council today. That should be made very clear, and any suggestion to the contrary is completely without foundation.
I might just say as well that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs asked why Canada should not have moved more quickly, the reality is that the Security Council did meet before August 25 and it would have been prudent and indeed desirable for Canada to have waited until the Security Council had moved, as it did ultimately move under 665, before proceeding to send troops into that area.
I might say as well that there is a great deal of hypocrisy in the response of many countries in this region. On July 31, two days before the invasion, the American government turned down efforts by a number of people in Congress to enforce trade sanctions against Iraq.
The Conservative government in November of last year was peddling all sorts of Canadian business at the Baghdad trade fair in November 1989 after the Iraqi government was responsible for the gassing, the chemical warfare against 4,000 Kurds in March 1988.
Following those comments, I want to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he in fact agrees that Canada should be playing a role at the Security Council to ensure that no country, including the United States, will in fact take unilateral offensive military action against Iraq outside the framework of the United
Nations and, more specifically, outside the framework of the Security Council.
It is essential that we have that assurance as a Parliament, because failing that assurance the lives of the many troops that have been sent into that area from Canada are put directly at risk. Is the Secretary of State for External Affairs prepared to give that assurance, and is he prepared to give the assurance that Canada will seek to establish a situation in which troops in the Middle East are there under United Nations command?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there were several questions there and some observations, including a confusion which I think I should elucidate, a confusion between a policy which would prevent the export of arms, which is what we are doing with regard to Iraq and to many other countries, and a policy which would say if there is behaviour that is objectionable to us we should stop all business with a country like Iraq.
I think it was that latter proposal that was put forward by the spokesman for the New Democratic Party. I think it important that that distinction be made because it would be unfortunate if we took attention away from the stand alone importance of the question of an effective arms embargo where we have to gather international support if we are going to make any progress. If we were suggesting a much broader approach which would say nobody does business with countries that behave in ways of which we disapprove, I can tell the hon. member he would know that our chances of success would not exist.
If I misinterpreted the amendment, which I only heard orally from his leader, then I apologize. I think that what she is saying, however, is that there should not have been a signal by Canada, that Canada should not have joined Egypt, should not have joined most of Europe, should not have joined Australia in sending a signal that would stop Saddam Hussein from carrying on his aggression. We do not think that it would be appropriate for Canada, as the Prime Minister said, to absent ourselves from our responsibility.
With respect to the member's particular question, we are working to ensure as much as we can, and ensure is a difficult word. We are using all of our influence to encourage all members of the world community to act within the framework of the United Nations. I have said that frequently in the House in this debate. That is
September 24, 1990

clearly what we are doing and that is the policy that we intend to follow. I reiterate to him that in order for us to be effective in pursuing that policy, it has to be clear to the rest of the world community that we are prepared not simply to talk about things, but that we are prepared also to deploy all our resources as they are appropriate: military, diplomatic, humanitarian.

Madam Speaker, I want to join in underlining the seriousness which the minister has echoed in his speech and make the following observation. The Secretary General in his comment indicated that we are possibly in the most serious situation of war since the Second World War. The Secretary of State for External Affairs says that imaginative options are being pursued. I would like to encourage him and others in that direction and suggest that we are dealing with face saving on two sides in this case. Canada is uniquely positioned with President Bush as well as with Hussein.
Second, the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke about humanitarian assistance and Canada's contribution. Former President Julius Nyreve today suggested in speaking to the south report that the by-product of this Iraqi situation will mean to the nations of the south some $18 billion to $26 billion on already fragile economies. In meeting with our Security Council members, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs bring this to their attention and see what the world community can do to offset the suffering implied in that?
Third, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has spoken about seizing this moment. For many years in the time of the East-West confrontation we have looked at a standing UN peace force. There have been designs and models and because of the East-West confrontation we have not been able to move. Will Canada now, and will the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his speech to the United Nations indicate that Canada will move to try to establish the machinery for a UN standing peace force with battalions held in reserve by national governments so that in an emergency like this or in another regional area we will not be beholden to one superpower or another to act and thereby the accusations that somehow the world community is not fully behind us?

Madam Speaker, for the purposes of this debate there were two main issues that faced Canadians this past summer. The first issue of course was the world crisis, possibly the most serious crisis that we faced certainly since the Korean War and possibly since the Second World War.
The first crisis was the world crisis and the threat. Canada responded to that in a way which we have learned in this debate not everybody appreciated.
The second issue that faced Canadians this past summer was a clear message from the people of Canada that they wanted to be consulted on what was happening in this country, in the governing of this country, and that they were going to hold all politicians, no matter what Parliament they served in, accountable for what was happening.
I contend that there were two crises: a growing threat of war and a growing threat of democracy. In dealing with the first issue, the growing threat of war, the government ignored the second issue, the growing threat of democracy. The government committed the Canadian Forces to the gulf with no consultation at all with Parliament or the people of Canada. There was consultation with the US. In fact the government reacted as a result of the request from the United States.
It was on August 6, the same day as the second resolution in the Security Council, that the Prime Minister went to Washington to consult with President Bush and there agreed to support the naval blockade in the gulf. Clearly Canada acted at the request and at the instigation of the United States, but at no time did Canada act in consultation with the Parliament or the people of Canada. This was unlike any other country with which we are associated now or with which we have been associated in the past. It was unlike, as my colleague from Winnipeg indicated earlier, Great Britain, which consulted its Parliament. It was unlike France. It was even unlike the United States because President George Bush, even when he was on the golf course, was consistently consulting and letting the people of the United States know what was happening and, indeed, consulting congressional leaders. He lives in a presidential system whereas we live in a parliamentary democracy. Unlike other parliamentary democracies with whom we are associated now and with whom we have been associated in the past, the government has not consulted Parliament and, through it, the Canadian people.
The government has said-that is the implied statement of the government-that this is not a serious enough issue on which to consult Parliament. It is not as serious as, for example, the parole bill for which Parliament was recalled some years ago. It was not as serious as the arrival of Tamils on the shores of Nova Scotia for
September 24, 1990

which Parliament was recalled in 1987. At that time the then Minister of Immigration said it was one of the most serious crises that Canada had faced and Parliament was recalled. But on this issue, which is the most serious issue which we have faced since the Korean War and, arguably, since the Second World War, there was no recall of Parliament.
That stands in stark contrast to the pattern of the past, of the entry into the Korean War for example. Parliament was sitting at the time in which Canada's participation was initiated, but Parliament prorogued for the summer and was recalled for an emergency session later to debate the entry into the Korean War.
So the practice this past summer is in stark contrast with what has happened before. We maintain that the government may have acted within the letter of the law as contained in the National Defence Act, but it has not acted within the spirit of the National Defence Act because that act clearly says that Parliament is to be recalled if Canadian forces are put on active service and if they are committed to a theatre of war. In doing so, we maintain that the government has compromised certainly the dignity and possibly the integrity of the Canadian Armed Forces because they had to change their plans to conform to the incompetent management of the Government of Canada.
It might be useful for us to recall some press clippings of the day that describe how the Canadian forces had to change their plan of action because of what they government was doing or, more importantly, not doing. Here is The Globe and Mail dated September 11:
Sources within the Canadian Forces say the government's commitment to the gulf has been consistently tempered by a reluctance to recall Parliament, and Defence Department spokesmen acknowledge that the ships' progress is tied to the date of Parliament's return.
Instead of sailing directly towards the Suez Canal and reaching the Red Sea early this week, the ship sought what department spokesmen called "other training opportunities-". The ships are currently in the Sicilian port of Augusta.
Asked whether there has been time for the ships to reach the Red Sea by now, navy spokesman Jeffrey Agnew said yesterday, "They could be there now. Yes."
Government Orders
However, the navy "scheduled a whole bunch of things" designed to ensure the ships did not arrive before Sept. 14. "Everything was back-dated from Sept. 24," he said.
A second department official, who did not wish to be named, said yesterday that the Canadian flotilla "is definitely not moving as quickly as possible."
Asked why the government did not order the ships to reach the Red Sea sooner and recall Parliament to authorize their status, Cmdr. Agnew said, "That is a political question, and not for me to discuss."
It is clear that there was a necessary change of plans by the Canadian Armed Forces to accommodate what the government was doing, or more importantly, not doing. Here is the report of that same time from Southam News.
Prime Minister Brian Mulroney's decision not to recall Parliament to debate the Persian Gulf crisis has temporarily stranded a convoy of three Canadian warships in Sicily.
Under the original timetable the three ships would not have been there until well after September 14.
But those plans fell apart on the weekend. On Saturday, Col. P.G. Boutet the defence department's chief judge and advocate, turned over a legal opinion concluding that the area of operation also included the Red Sea.
After being told that cabinet would not sign the order until Sept. 15, senior military officials decided to delay the ships which originally would have entered the Red Sea on Sept. 13 or earlier.
So it is very clear that the handling of this by the Government of Canada necessitated a change in plans by the Canadian Armed Forces. What signal does that send about the seriousness of our intent? What signal does it send to our allies? What signal does it send to the Canadian people? What signal does it send to the people in Halifax? What signal does it send to the spouses of Canadian forces personnel who went down to the jetties and who tied yellow ribbons in remembrance of those people who were going overseas. There are people in this House today who stood with them on the jetties and who understood the seriousness of what they were doing, who understood that this was a matter of duty for anybody in the Canadian forces. They did this willingly with a seriousness of purpose, with great sympathy, great compassion and with great sadness, only to discover that those ships spent two days off course, going through unnecessary manoeuvres because of the handling of this situation by the Government of Canada.

September 24, 1990
Government Orders
Those are the kinds of things that Canadians cannot tolerate and cannot appreciate. The Government of Canada may have acted within the letter of the law because the letter of the law says, if you put Canadian forces on active duty you have to recall Parliament within 10 days. But the spirit of the law clearly is that Parliament is to be consulted.
I maintain that if we have learned anything over this past summer it is that the people of Canada not only want that consultation but demand it. If there is one message coming through clearly after this past summer it is that the people of Canada want to know what the government is doing. More than that, they want to participate in what the government is doing and what is happening in this country. That is what the government failed to recognize. They followed the letter of the law of the National Defence Act, but they did not follow the spirit of the National Defence Act.
What will the government do? This question was raised by my colleague from Winnipeg just a few moments ago. I am not sure we have received an entirely clear answer as to what the government will do. We know what the government has done thus far and we know how the government has operated thus far. They have operated without consulting Parliament and without consulting the Canadian people.
Our sea forces are in the Gulf. They are under the aegis of the UN because of the resolutions that have been passed. But there are other forces on land in the Gulf which are not under the aegis of the United Nations. What happens if there is a declaration of war? What happens if the United States declares war? What will be the position of the Government of Canada then, and how will the Government of Canada act? I think Canadians want to have a clear answer to that question. I am not sure that we got a clear answer from the Secretary of State for External Affairs this afternoon.
While the people of Canada support the containment of aggression and the establishment of peace, they do not support Canada simply being an appendage of the United States. The people of Canada want an independent posture for this country. We are still an independent country and the people of Canada will want an independent posture and not simply a yes-man role for
the government. The government has to give a very clear answer to that question. I think the government has to give a very clear answer to that question.
Another matter the government has to give a clear answer to, and I have not heard it this afternoon yet, is what initiatives were taken in the Security Council to promote a peaceful resolution. In the past Canada has given a good account of itself in that forum but I ask the question, where is the equivalent of Lester Pearson today.
During the Suez crisis a Canadian was prominent in not only bringing about an important solution to a world problem but being seen to bring about an important solution to a world problem. Where is that same Canadian today? Where is that same leadership today? If in fact Canada is taking that kind of leadership in the Security Council, we do not know about it. There is no evidence. The Canadian people do not know about it, Parliament does not know about it. Exactly what has Canada done and exactly what is Canada doing within the Security Council to bring about a peaceful resolution of this? Now is the time to strengthen the UN. There is a window of opportunity.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs said a moment ago, out of this crisis may come a strengthened UN. That is the hope of us all, but unless we work we cannot expect that to happen willy-nilly. We cannot expect that to happen inadvertently. We have to work at strengthening the UN. We have to ask again: what is the role of the Canadian government in this?
In conclusion I would like to say that Canadians are encouraged by the role that the UN has played in this crisis and we must seize this opportunity to assert the primacy of the UN. Second, Canadians abhor and deplore the actions of Iraq. We must underscore and emphasize that this party and the people of Canada, and indeed this House deplore what has happened in the Persian Gulf, deplore the aggression of Iraq. Canadians want an independent policy. They want to see that we are not simply an appendage of the United States but that we have a clear, national policy of our own.
Last, and above all, Canadians want to know what are the government's plans. They want to be consulted about

those plans and participate in the formulation of them. That has not happened up to now. It must happen now and in the future.

Madam Speaker, I have a comment. I have listened intently and I perhaps have a bit of a personal interest that some other people in the House do not have in this issue.
Wait a minute. I have that interest.

Of the three naval vessels that were ordered overseas by the Prime Minister, at least half, and perhaps a few more, of those men and women who are serving come from my riding. So, as everybody gets into the sterile debate as to whether or not this or that was done at the right time, I would like the government to understand quite clearly that it is not dealing with just pawns on a chessboard here. It is dealing with men and women who have been trained to serve in the Canadian Armed Forces. But, more importantly, it is dealing with the families of those men and women who have been trained to serve in the Canadian Armed Force and who, for love of country, have decided to make this a career.
I have to tell the Speaker that I was not just annoyed, but I was highly insulted by the manner in which this government treated those families. What this government did was unconscionable. What it did was unprecedented. It ordered Canadian naval vessels to the Persian Gulf area. That perhaps in itself may be open to debate. I happen to think that Canada had a role to play.
I listened intently to the Prime Minister when he spoke earlier. He said that it acted against what was a flagrant abuse of international law. He was talking about Iraq, obviously. He said that was why the Canadian Forces were ordered in. I do not have a debate with that particular point, but let us take it a little further.
The Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs and others have talked at great length about why we did what we did, but there is a double-edged sword here. The people of Canada want to talk

Government Orders
about what they did not do, and what they did not do was keep the Canadian public informed through the proper forum and that was the floor of the House of Commons. They did not keep the men and women who were serving, the men and women who might be ordered over to serve, or their families, their loved ones, and their neighbours informed. What had to happen was that those individuals in my riding had to turn on the CNN evening news every night and watch George Bush on a golf course chatting between yells of "fore" or "Brian"-whichever one it was-to find out exactly what was going on. That is something the people in my riding and the people of the Canadian Armed Forces are not going to forget easily.
I know that you are telling me that my time is just about up, Madam Speaker, but this is an important point. I am speaking for a lot of individuals whose loved ones may be the first casualties if something happens in the Middle East and they want to see a debate in the House of Commons. They want the government called to account for why it did not inform the Canadian public through Parliament. But, more importantly, the day that those navy vessels went out, I and my colleague from Halifax sat down on the Halifax waterfront and watched those three naval vessels going out. We watched the Sea King helicopters flying past. We watched those men and women waving goodbye, many of them wondering if they were ever going to return.
There was something wrong there that day because, although we have an unprecedented engagement of Canadian naval vessels, the Prime Minister of Canada was not even there to see the men and women that he sent off to a potential theatre of war. That is something, if we do get to debate this a little later tonight, that I want to go into more detail. I want to go back very briefly to what my colleague from Labrador has said.
He talked about the need for this place to have been informed much sooner than what we have had to wait and I think that that is the debate that we should be having here tonight. We all understand the severity of the situation in the Middle East. We all understand our role within the United Nations, or at least we should. We all understand the potential for major disaster in the activities that are now taking place or have taken place
in the Middle East. But we should also understand that this government was absolutely negligent in its responsibility to the Canadian public.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member for Labrador who has just spoken a question with respect to the resolution of this very difficult conflict. Obviously, we join in calling for the unconditional withdrawal by Iraq from Kuwait. Under United Nations command, hopefully, through sanctions and the effective enforcement of those sanctions, we will be able to persuade Iraq to withdraw.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Labrador about the longer term and what the position of his party is with respect to one of the very serious issues that must be addressed in the longer term in this region. Indeed, even Secretary of State James Baker said before Congress last month that he recognized that this is an issue that must be addressed. I speak, of course, of the question of the tragic plight of the Palestinians and, of course, the hypocrisy of the Americans. On the one hand they are saying that we must enforce united resolutions when they agree with them, but on the other hand, they are refusing to call upon Israel to accept Resolution 242.
Therefore, does the hon. member for Labrador agree that an essential part of the longer-term resolution of this tragic conflict must be the convening of an international conference at which all of those parties who are directly affected-including the Palestinians and their representatives, the Palestine Liberation Organization-will participate and recognize the right of self-determination of the Palestinians, their right to a state and, of course, the right of Israel to exist within secure borders? Does his party support that very important position?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say that I have been in the House and observed from outside the debate that has taken place to this point on the motion that has been put forward. I must again say that I am pleased to be able to address that motion concerning the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq.
I want to focus briefly on Canada's response and, in particular, the decision to commit elements of Canadian forces in the Persian Gulf area. It is fair to say that we all recognize that this is a serious commitment of the government on behalf of Canada. Canada has taken a stand, along with other civilized nations in the world, against this brutal act of aggression against Kuwait.
I would like to take a moment, if I could, to explain the purpose of the Order in Council which I tabled earlier this day. The government believes that it is important to respect the longstanding tradition of the parliamentary system and that the deployment abroad of armed forces be debated in the House of Commons. This tradition is rooted in the history of the place. It stretches back almost 90 years to when Canada first sent troops to the Boer War. Over the years we have debated in the House and approved the deployment of Canadian forces abroad. The last time a deployment of this significance took place was in 1950 when the Government of Canada committed Canadian troops to take part in the United Nations peace-restoring or peace-making effort in Korea.
Once again, the world is faced with a flagrant act of aggression, a violation of international law and civilized values and, once again, Canada must stand up and be counted among those civilized countries opposing this act of aggression. Taking an easy position is not Canada's way. It has not been our history to seek the easy or the peaceful area to expound our beliefs. Traditionally, Canadians, men and women who serve this country, have been involved in the difficult decisions in the hard places
Government Orders
to show our belief in values and our belief that aggression cannot be tolerated.
As the Prime Minister said on August 10, the lessons of history are clear. Timing a blind eye to aggression only encourages further aggression. No civilized nation is excused from its broader responsibilities to the world community for international peace and order. If a clear warning is not sent to Iraq now, it will serve only to embolden it to find a new victim.
At the outset, the deployment of the elements of the Canadian forces represents a serious commitment by the government. Parliament has an important role to play. Parliament can be veiy helpful, the men and women assembled here and representing constituencies around Canada. Parliament, by being united, can send a strong message to the Iraqi government that we do not tolerate aggression. If we are united in the House, I suggest, as has the member from Halifax who was concerned about his constituents, we can best send a strong message of support to those men and women who are serving their country abroad.
I would suggest to all members of the House that there be support for the actions that have been taken. We ask for the approval of a strong Canadian commitment, not just words, not seeking a peaceful area, but taking a stand as we have historically and as we, as Canadians, have recognized in the past as being important.
There are basic international principles that we believe we uphold. I ask my colleagues in the House to consider the gravity of Iraq's action. I ask them to consider what would happen if the suggestion was that we should do nothing and the message that would send, that Canada would refuse to join a multinational military effort to enforce the sanctions of the United Nations. It would be fine to have those sentiments but not act. It would be fine to talk tough and not act. But it certainly would not be in the tradition of Canada and it certainly would not be in the tradition of the men and women who serve now and have served in the past.
I would suggest that there is a place for diplomatic actions and it has been actively pursued. We have heard in the House from colleagues who have identified those actions which have been taken by Canada's Ambassador to the United Nations to bring forward these resolutions

September 24, 1990
Government Orders
from 661 to 665. Those resolutions imposed the embargo and allowed nations with maritime force in the area to enforce the embargo.
Over the past number of weeks, there have been changes that have taken place. As a matter of fact, before Kuwait was attacked by Iraq, the Government of Iraq assured its Arab neighbours, and in particular President Mubarak from Egypt, that it would not attack its smaller neighbour, that it was only interested in a peaceful resolution. Quickly it broke off talks and annexed the small country of Kuwait.
This was done by a country that has, I would suggest, more military might than is needed for the defence of its own borders. It was done by a country that has waged an eight-year war against its neighbour. It was done by a country that placed under the pretext of negotiations some 150,000 troops on the border between Iraq and Kuwait, some 1,200 tanks, some 1,000 armoured personnel carriers while it was carrying on a facade of negotiating with a smaller and less militarily strong nation.
What we have at this time is a presence of Canadian forces in the Persian Gulf area to take place on position approximately October 1 or October 2. Ultimately we have to recognize the actions that were taken by the government, by the men and women who serve to ready themselves for this activity.
What we have and what we have committed are military forces in the Persian Gulf region to support an international effort to deter the aggression of Iraq and to enforce the sanctions that were applied under the United Nations.
Canada has believed and will continue to believe that there must be, if possible, a peaceful resolution of dispute. I suggest to my colleagues in the House that the actions that were taken initially after Iraq invaded Kuwait stopped that aggression where it only gobbled up one small country and did not continue in gobbling up its neighbours in the Persian Gulf area.
There has to be respect for the sanctity of existing states, borders and their citizens, and that is part of the mission of the Canadian forces along with the forces from some 25 other nations in this world.
There has been a suggestion that Canada made a decision because we were following the lead of other countries. Canada made a decision because what took place offended the sensibilities of Canadians. What took place offended the reality of today, and it is not just Canada. It is the United States. It is the U.S.S.R. It is Egypt. It is Australia. It is Afghanistan that my colleagues should understand. It is Bangladesh. It is Pakistan that has made commitments to stop aggression and to enforce the sanctions of the United Nations.
This is not something that is usual in the course of the United Nations. In the past, we have wished to see the United Nations act in a more determined manner, and it has been unable to do so. At this point with the action, co-operation and leadership in several cases of Canada, the United Nations has strengthened itself and has put in place sanctions that we believe are important, that we believe if Iraq understands the world condemnation will have it returned to the borders prior to its attack, to have it allow the citizens who it is detaining returned to their countries and to stop any further aggression by Iraq. There are a couple of things that have been accomplished by Saddam Hussein. I am not too sure that they are accomplishments that we would applaud, but at this time he has concentrated his forces on the borders of Saudi Arabia, threatening not only Saudi Arabia but the gulf states, Bahrain, Qatar, United Arab Emirates. He has, as I mentioned earlier, constrained citizens of other countries from leaving. He has threatened to use citizens of other countries as a shield, a sign of a true bully and a true bully who is a coward.
The effect of the embargo and the determination of Canada and other countries which are presently there is hope for the world. There has been a suggestion that Canada and the men and women who are serving do not have a definite mission. I think it is important to redefine again the mission.
The mission is that Canada has joined with other countries of the world, some 25, to deter further aggression and to enforce the sanctions of the United Nations. To this goal we despatched the three ships, Alhabaskan, Terra Nova and Protecteur, and almost 1,000 Canadian men and women. The preparation for that departure was concluded in a very brief period of time. I compliment the men and women, both in and out of uniform, who accomplished a goal that was at some point recognized

as being heroic. Their work and their dedication are an important aspect of this and should not be forgotten. But we had some work to do and we had it accomplished.
We have put new systems on the vessels, the Javelin anti-air missile, the Phalanx close-in system as well as 50 and 40 calibre millimetre anti-aircraft guns. We were able to deploy on August 24 and they entered the Red Sea on September 16 and within a 24-hour period will pass through the Straits of Hormuz.
We also made another decision to send a squadron of CF-18 fighter jets from the Canadian Forces base in Baden. We are currently discussing with the countries in the area as to the location of our air force but that will be concluded in a very short period of time. That again involves the deployment of some 450 plus Canadian personnel to support this operation. But the role of our vessels which has been recognized as that of enforcing sanctions against Iraq will be through surveillance, through monitoring and, if necessary, interception of ships to verify their cargoes and their destinations.
Under Security Council resolution 665 our maritime forces are authorized to use such measures as may be necessary to halt all inward and outward shipping to ensure that the sanctions are not being violated. The CF-18s will provide long-range defence air cover in the operating area of the Canadian task group and will be part of an integrated multinational air defence network in the gulf area. Together with those defensive resources of other countries, our CF-18s will investigate unidentified or hostile aircraft and ships that could be capable of attacking the Canadian task group or other allied ships. They will also investigate any unknown radar contacts and take appropriate action to protect the men and women on Canadian ships.
On September 9 and 10 Canada took part in the naval conference in Bahrain to discuss co-operation among the various nations involved.
The purpose of that meeting was to allocate operational sectors within which each nation could operate within the Red Sea, the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf.
For a number of reasons, military reasons-I refer this to my friend from the NDP-these were decisions made
Government Orders
by military leadership for the safety and security of Canadian men and women. The place they could do their best work was in the Persian Gulf area. They could do that work in co-operation with other countries and they would end up having the benefit, not only of Canadian support, but the support of other allied countries in an over-all umbrella and an over-all activity within a region.
The hon. member from the New Democratic Party asked: "Who is in command"? The forces that are deployed are under Canadian command and control at all times and they will remain under Canadian command and control at all times.
I do not know whether the hon. member understands the significance of that. Canadians have long ago given up the right to another country or another jurisdiction to command and control our men and women who are deployed on behalf of the people of Canada in any conflict around the world.
Madam Speaker, the questions as to the risk are serious. There is risk in any activity involving forces. Indeed, today there is more risk involved in this activity probably than there has been at any time since the Korean war. That risk was weighed. It was not weighed by politicians. It was weighed by military leadership. That risk was assessed as being acceptable.
I want to give colleagues some idea as to how that decision was arrived at. Yes, Iraq has a very impressive standing army of some 5,000 main battle tanks, but these land forces do not pose a significant risk to Canadian air and naval operations in the region. The Iraqi air force has approximately 500 combat aircraft. The navy, on the other hand, consists of a small number of frigates and coastal patrol craft. Both the Iraqi navy and air force are equipped with anti-ship missiles.
I want to take a minute to talk about the defensive capabilities. In addition to the active defence systems that were put on the task group before it left Halifax, our ships have new passive defensive including mine detector sonars, chaff dispersers and air search radars. The Terra Nova has been fitted with harpoon surface-to-surface missiles. These systems will enable our vessels to defend themselves against a potential missile threat and thus fulfil their role in the Persian Gulf.

September 24, 1990
Government Orders
With the Phalanx anti-aircraft guns and missiles as well as the passive defence systems we should be able to effectively operate against any threat posed by the Iraqi anti-ship missiles.
The squadron of CF-18s which has been deployed will also help in the defence of our vessels. The pilots and ground personnel which will be drawn mostly from Europe are trained and experienced. They are experienced in multinational air defence operations. Indeed, some have already trained with the task group as it proceeded into the gulf area.
I believe one of the most difficult things to defend against and one of the weapons that Canadians have difficulty in understanding is that of chemical warfare.
I am not too sure what the comment was from the New Democratic Party. I am sure they will have a chance to speak later.
I want to assure Canadians and I want to bring to the attention of the families of the men and women who are serving that even though the Iraqis have been ruthless in the use of chemical weaponry-They have used it against their own people, the Kurdish minority in their country. They it used in Iran-we have assessed the chemical threat. We have taken steps to ensure that we will be able to meet that threat.
Those steps are involved with the external sprinkling system. They are the opportunity to rinse off the contamination, the opportunity to seal off our vessels and pressurize compartments, and all crew members have been provided with individual protection suits and gas masks. In the CF-18 in the aircraft area there is also the protection that is necessary against possible chemical attack.
I know you are giving me the time signal, Madam Speaker, but I believe it is important to take a minute in closing to talk about the over-all defensive capability of our task force. It will be enhanced by other task groups in the area, and it will be enhanced by the co-operation of those groups. Some naval forces possess longer range detection and defensive systems against aircraft and missiles than Canadian vessels do.
All these factors, I suggest to you, Madam Speaker, have made the risk acceptable. That does not mean that it should be taken lightly. That does not mean that we should discount it, but I believe with the co-operation of both naval and air and in co-operation with allied forces in the region in this multinational effort we will be able
to ensure that those men and women have the best protection that Canada can provide, the best opportunity to bring about a successful conclusion of their mission which, again I reiterate, is to enforce the sanctions levied by the United Nations and to deter any further aggression.
Canada has been a long-standing member of the United Nations, and we would not be expected at this time to relegate ourselves to a minor role in an important task that has been designed and debated.
I say in closing that under Canadian command and control the provision of our co-operative efforts in a multinational effort we are contributing to the longstanding aims and goals of the Canadian foreign policy. We are supporting actively the United Nations. We believe that it is in the true historic tradition of Canada that we do take tough decisions, that our men and women serve well, and that we do not and will not tolerate aggression.

Madam Speaker, I think it is no mystery to my colleagues that I know that part of the world pretty well, if I may say so. I do not wish to underestimate this knowledge nor to overestimate it. It is quite complex. I will certainly take part in the debate to come.
I can think of a few points I would like my hon. colleagues to ponder over.
As one who, in his long career, has had the honour to travel in most of those countries and to put out a number of fires, I can tell you that I have always been careful for some reason. I did not make any concessions, that would have been out of character for me. I have yet to visit Lybia and Saudi Arabia. Those are about the only countries left for me to visit in that area.
I spoke before the Parliament of Kuwait in the days when it existed, that is before it was dissolved by the Emir. It is rather unusual for a North-American parle-mentarian to speak there.
I have learned one thing though. One may know when and how he entered the Middle-East, but let me remind you that, according to another proverb, one never knows when or how he will get out of the Middle-East. Please think about it before we get into the debate.
Since the beginning of the debate, especially as regards our neighbours and friends to the South, I have found outrageous all the new and dreadfull names used, the sudden equation Hussein-Hitler. I have no intent to defend Mr. Saddam Hussein. I have met him, but I will not stand up for him. I am surprised however by such sudden discovery of who he is and by how suddenly people came to realize that he is armed with the most destructive weapons in the world. His nuclear capacity is not as strong as that of Israel, I agree, but chemical and bacteriological weapons do cause disasters. Let us keep in mind, when the time comes to debate that question, that many young people risk being killed by the very weapons that there own countries, be it France or another country, have sold to Irak.
Government Orders
What I want to ask the minister has to do with the new war logic. French President Mitterand keeps saying that we are on the verge of endorsing war logic principles. My esteemed colleague and friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Axworthy), my Party's new critic on Canadian foreign affairs, is a brilliant man fully conversant with such issues. He knows that when people talk about a war logic-I direct my remarks to the Minister of National Defence-they seem to forget that there should also be a peace logic. Obviously the minister stated that we will do our share. The Prime Minister made a few comments, superlative as usual. I suggest that Canada's contribution should be made at the diplomatic level.
My question to the minister is precise: other than this war logic which, we are told, seems to fascinate all nations of the world, is there a peace logic to which Canada would more readily subscribe? I think I will make a suggestion, the first. Referring to countries like Canada, Algeria, Senegal, India, I ask the Minister of National Defence whether his department and the Department of External Affairs now have a committee considering the best contribution Canada might make to this debate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague puts forward an important question and I understand the dilemma in which he finds himself, as others in the House may find themselves.
He asked a specific question: Is there a group or are we in the Department of National Defence and in the Department of External Affairs looking at other things that Canada can do to bring about a peaceful resolution?
Yes, Mr. Speaker. At the outset, Canada, through its ambassador and its seat on the Security Council, has been focusing on the involvement of the United Nations in this action, not one country but the United Nations, and we are continuing to work in that manner. Both our departments, if I could say to my colleague, would welcome and are working toward and imploring the United Nations to put a blue flag over the whole of the multinational effort. That is what Canada would like to see, but we cannot wait for the United Nations to make that decision because, as we know, in the past the United Nations at times has not been able to arrive at a decision. If he is asking about the efforts, both government

Adjournment Debate
departments, in fact the whole of government, would welcome that initiative and are working toward it in the United Nations. Hopefully we will be successful.

Mr. Speaker, first of all the House should know that we fully support our troops and the men and women who are there. What we have some difficulty with is the clarity of the government's policy in this area. I would just like to ask the minister for some very specific and clear commitments to this House.
He has said that the troops are under Canadian command, and he said that very emphatically. I would like to know what directions the government has given to the commanding officers in the Persian Gulf in respect of the outer limits of their mandate.
A retired rear-admiral in the United States has given quite an excerpt on the view of the American government, that it is moving into an offensive build up in the Middle East. Many other military analysts have said the Americans are preparing for an offensive assault on Iraq that at this stage has no UN sanction whatever. The chief of staff of the United States Air Force was fired because he made it veiy clear publicly that the Americans were building up an offensive capacity in the gulf.
UN resolution 665 which the government has relief on in support of its direction of our troops into that area very specifically calls on members states to deal with the necessary military involvement to "halt all inward and outward maritime shipping in order to inspect and verily their cargoes and to ensure strict compliance with the provisions related to such shipping laid down in UN resolution 661".
My question is very specific. Will the minister assure this House and the country that the government has given clear direction to the commanding officers of the Canadian contingent in the gulf that they are not to participate in any offensive action in the gulf and that their mandate for military involvement is not to exceed the terms of reference of resolution 661?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If I can be brief, Mr. Speaker, we have not given definitive direction, as the member asks, that their terms of reference will not exceed 661.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Then 665. That is different.
There is another thing that we have continually said, that we are also there to deter further aggression. That is part of the mission that has been given to the Canadians who are serving. They are given the ability, and their rules of engagement will not deter from their ability to defend themselves. The assurance that I can give the hon. member is that they do not have their ability for self-defence deterred by the rules of engagement that they have been given.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on this first day back in session because I was extremely dissatisfied with an answer given to me by this government during Question Period.
In her answer to me the minister responsible for the status of women said that violence against women was her top priority. Yet she and her government have put a spending limit on the Canada Assistance Plan, the federal-provincial funding mechanism for shelters for battered women.
Three provinces were singled out for this spending limit. My own province of British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario. The Minister for National Health and Welfare replied to my question about CAP by saying that only the rich provinces are affected by this spending limit.
Well I said, Mr. Speaker, that the women in British Columbia who are battered are just as battered and bruised as any abused women in this country. Their pain is real. It makes no difference to them when they are being battered that they live in a so-called have province.
Currently the government says it is spending a fortune, a lot of dollars on battered women, and the figures that it releases does sound like a lot of money until you realize that this figure is spread out over four years and that much of it is spent on research and not on shelter spaces.

The figure amounts to $10 per year per battered woman. One of every two women who seeks shelter at a refuge for battered women is turned away because there is no space for her. These women often have small children and the shelter is their last resort. There is nowhere for them to turn except to the streets or to go back to the abuser.
A woman and her children usually arrive at a shelter when all of their options have been exhausted. She has already tried her family and her friends. She does not have the money for a hotel or an apartment. And this government claps itself on the back and says what a wonderful job it is doing for battered women.
The legislation that puts a spending limit on CAP passed the House of Commons and is now in the Senate. The Prime Minister is currently attempting to stuff the Senate with Tory appointees so that the CAP legislation and other legislation will go through quickly.
What we are seeing in this country is a level of patronage appointments that is unprecedented. Canadians are sickened by this display by the Tory Prime Minister. We have had a summer of discontent in Canada, a difficult summer for all Canadians, and our Prime Minister refused to recall Parliament to deal with these issues.
Now the Prime Minister wants to shut down Parliament, shut down this session as soon as possible. In this way he and his government can avoid their responsibility to Parliament and their responsibility to Canadians, the responsibility with the crisis at Oka, the responsibility with the Persian Gulf crisis on which we have heard debate today, the responsibility over GST and all of the Tory unpopular policies.
My constituents in New Westminster and Burnaby elected me to represent them on important issues facing them and affecting British Columbians and other Canadians. The Prime Minister is thwarting democracy by attempting to stifle the voices of members of Parliament and not listening to the Canadian public. This whole affair not only shows that the Prime Minister and his government have no commitment to the poor, to the children, and to battered women in this country, but also no real commitment to Senate reform.
New Democrats have been offered Senate seats in the past and they have always turned them down. They have
Adjournment Debate
turned them down because New Democrats do not believe in a non-accountable body and people living on the public purse without accountability to the people.
Under a New Democratic Party government you would not see British Columbians singled out for punishment in this matter. You would not see social assistance, child care, shelters for battered women choked off by capping the Canada Assistance Plan.
A recent National Council of Welfare report showed that 60 per cent of the poor in Canada are women. In British Columbia the federal and the provincial governments are collaborating to ensure that they and their children do not have enough to eat.
One in five Canadian children is poor. New Democrats have outlined ways to ease this poverty with a view to eliminating it in the long term.
There are two foods banks in my constituency. Poverty is a national disgrace. It affects seniors, single parent families, children, the disabled and the working poor.
Children are the largest users of food banks in this country. In a country as rich as ours, it should be a crime to choke off social assistance and child care programs as well as programs to aid women who are victims of violence.
We need programs that will help people to get back on their feet again, not inadequate programs that dole out money once in a while. Literacy, job training and counselling are all necessary to help people become self-sufficient.
Shelters for battered women funded through CAP are not simply a roof over the heads of victims of violence, although that is extremely important. They help the woman to find a job, housing, schools or child care for their children. They provide the counselling that tells the woman what she most needs to hear, that she is a valuable human being and that she does not deserve abuse. She needs to hear that help is available and that others in our society do care.
The shelters refer women to doctors or lawyers who they may need. They offer support groups and a new start on life. These are the programs that this government wants curtailed. Other programs funded by CAP

do not even have the chance to develop the way the shelter program has.
The goal of all social assistance should be to help people to become self-sufficient again, to break the cycle of poverty and not to reinforce it.
I call on this government to stop this legislation and to put a ceiling on the Canada Assistance Plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, strange though it may seem, I would like to thank the hon. member for Westminster-Burnaby for giving me a chance to respond to her question about what the government is doing about its priority on fighting family violence.
The hon. member knows perfectly well that since May 14,1990, when she asked this question, there have been a number of unprecedented events in this country, including, Mr. Speaker-and unfortunately she is right-the events in Oka, in my riding, and in Chateauguay, as a result of which there was no mention of the women and children murdered over a period of five weeks. Mr. Speaker, family violence is taking on alarming proportions.
She said that the Budget proposals would cap increases in payments to Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia at 5 per cent.
She also referred to unpopular measures our government must take. I think she may be right. We are taking unpopular measures in order to curb the deficit, so that we can keep essential programs like those that deal with family violence.
She ought to know that more than one billion in real dollars, and I repeat "real", will be paid under the Canada Assistance Plan during the current fiscal year, and this is only for provincial programs designed for victims of violence.
There is one very important program, Project Haven, under which $22 billion has been earmarked over a period of four years, across the country, to create new spaces for women and children who are victims of family violence. In my own riding, la Maison Citadelle in Lachute has been involved in this program, and we have been able to allocate about $200,000 for the construction of new beds.
Mr. Speaker, I wish the program did not exist, because that would mean there are no women or children who are victims of family violence. Unfortunately, the reality in this country is quite different.
I can inform the House that the Department's program for shelters has been very successful. Of course it is not enough. We would need $44 million. However, I would urge the hon. member and all members of this House to speak out against violence and try to help both men who are violent and women who are victims of family violence.
