speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last March I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development a question about the latest annual report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. The Human Rights Commission in 1988 referred to the situation of aboriginal people in this country as a national tragedy. Last year the commission said it had no reason to alter that judgment.
I asked the minister last March what immediate action the government was prepared to take to turn this tragedy around. The minister gave the standard government response. He referred to how much money the government was spending and to certain areas of current government activities. At the same time he acknowledged that further improvement in the conditions of aboriginal people is required.
What has the government done since then to further improve the conditions of aboriginal people? We have seen no improvement whatsoever. In fact, the government has managed to make matters even worse, as the events of this summer and the Oka crisis have shown.
The Human Rights Commission's 1989 annual report called for a new deal for the aboriginal people of this country, based on the commitment by non-aboriginal Canadians to meaningful political and cultural autonomy and much greater economic self-sufficiency. To date the government has not shown any evidence of such a commitment, despite the growing body of advice it has received on the direction it should be taking.
September 24, 1990

In 1983 the report of the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government provided a clear direction to the government with respect to aboriginal self-government. In 1985 the Task Force on Comprehensive Claims Policy outlined several new directions for the government in the interest of reaching fair and equitable land claim settlements. The major recommendations of these reports have been ignored.
Aboriginal leaders have tried over the years to focus the attention of the government on aboriginal issues. Time and time again the government has been warned that the current conditions are intolerable and cannot be allowed to continue and that the patience of the aboriginal people is running out. Time and time again the government has not listened. The government has refused to make the abysmal social and economic conditions of aboriginal people a priority on the national agenda. Unacceptable conditions in a western industrialized country as rich as Canada are allowed to persist.
With the World Summit for Children coming up this weekend, it is appropriate to remind the House of how badly the government has failed Canada's aboriginal children. Aboriginal people are the poorest of the poor in this country. Poor health and early deaths are among the consequences of aboriginal poverty.
Last year the Canadian Institute of Child Health published a report on Canada's children. That report described once again the continuing inequalities between aboriginal and non-aboriginal people. A newborn child in the Canadian population as a whole is expected to live 76 years. A newborn aboriginal child has a life expectancy of 68 years. Infant morality rates among aboriginal people are double the national average. Suicide rates among aboriginal people are many times higher than the national Canadian average.
According to the report of the Child Health Institute, when it comes to the health of aboriginal children we have Third World problems within our society.
The Prime Minister will be co-chairing the World Summit for Children and I suggest that this government and this country cannot be part of the existing and continuing disparities between aboriginal and non-aboriginal Canadians. In addition to any concerted action on aboriginal social and economic issues, the government
Adjournment Debate
has steadfastly refused to deal with the fundamental political issues which are at the root of this country's relationship with its aboriginal peoples.
Justice for aboriginal people in the country has been delayed and denied over and over again. Lands claimed by aboriginal people continue to be eliminated even when negotiations are proceeding. Logging and forms of resource development are allowed to continue on lands which aboriginal people have not given up. Throughout the country aboriginal people continue to be harassed in the exercise of their aboriginal hunting and trapping rights in violation of their rights, court decisions, and the Constitution of Canada.
Under this government, post-secondary education was capped and many aboriginal students were denied the opportunity to pursue higher education. Aboriginal constitutional negotiations were terminated by this government. With this history of neglect, the government should not be surprised that the aboriginal people and many other Canadians believe the government has failed them.
In conclusion, the government will continue to fail aboriginal people as long as it insists on its present course. Fundamental change is needed now. Aboriginal people need justice and political action from this government, not platitudes.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with my hon. colleague that there is a long way to go in Canada in the treatment of our Indian and native peoples, but in fact the government is committed to making changes. I think we should put the question into perspective and talk a little bit about some of the advances that have been made over the last 18 years or so.
We are committed to progress in all the areas that the hon. member has mentioned. Some of that progress has been made, and more will be made, through co-operation with the Indian people and the Inuit people themselves. In fact, Mr. Yalden pointed out in his own report that significant improvements have been made over the past several years.

Adjournment Debate
Our government is absolutely committed to strengthening the capacity of Indian peoples to provide their own government and to design systems that will be flexible to serve the needs of the communities that we are dealing with-programs that are really designed to meet the individual needs of the Indian and Inuit people who are involved, rather than quite as bureaucratic as has been perhaps in the past.
Steady progress has been achieved in transferring control of program expenditures to Indians over the past 18 years as I have mentioned. For example, in 1971, Indians managed only 20 per cent of the budgets that were set aside for their use. In 1990-1991, Indians will manage over 72 per cent of these budgets and that counts for over $1 billion in their hands for the delivery of services to Indian and Inuit peoples across the country.
Substantial progress is also being made in other areas. For example, in education, only 53 band-operated schools existed in 1975, but some five times more than that number, 280, existed last year in 1989. Enrolment in post-secondary education in 1989 had increased over 35 per cent from 1985. Contrary to interpretations that were put upon this in the report, post-secondary education budgets were actually increased very significantly to $149 million.
In the area of child welfare, there is no question that there is a need for improvement and that has been recognized. Therefore, in co-operation with Indian leadership, the federal government has entered into arrangements whereby Indian-operated child welfare agencies provide child and family services for many Indian communities. These are agencies operated by the people themselves.
Economic self-sufficiency for aboriginal people is also a priority. It is a priority for the government. This is evidenced by the establishment of the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy, or CAEDS as it is more commonly known. This strategy is a very positive initiative aimed at helping Indian and Inuit people to build their own economic structure.
In collaboration with Indian people, changes to the Indian Act are being considered. Through the lands, revenues and trust review, there is collaboration that will bring about changes that will recognize Indian authority over their own lands and money and the governance of these.
Another priority is the development of community-based self-government. The objectives of this initiative are to enhance community control and decision making and to recognize all those diverse needs and traditions that are there. Currently eight projects involving 30 bands are in negotiations. Fifteen projects involving 29 bands are working more closely toward framework agreements and over 100 bands are at the initial state of defining what community development and government means to them.
I know there is a long way to go on the issues that the hon. member mentioned, but the government is committed to achieving those goals and with co-operation and collaboration we will do so.

speakerposition: subtopic
N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, education, in all its aspects is, and should be, a right of all Canadians. Post-secondary education is increasingly a necessity in today's fast-paced and ever-changing world. Because of this, it is essential to the welfare of Canadians and Canada to ensure that Canadians from all backgrounds are given the opportunity to attend a post-secondary education institution if they have the ability to do so and if they wish to do so. This, unfortunately, is not the case.
As Canada is a mosaic of different people from different backgrounds and cultures, so must be our education system. More must be done to include those with lower incomes, women, native peoples, visible minorities, and Francophones outside of Quebec. Not only are these groups presently under-represented in our post-secondary education institutions, but they are also hurt the most when government funding is cut and tuition fees increase.
Although advances have been made in the past 25 years, the great majority of potential students in Canada still do not attend a post-secondary education institution. Research shows that a disproportionate number of university students have an upper or upper-middle class socioeconomic background. Much potential talent remains under-developed in other socioeconomic groups. Higher fees, along with rising living expenses and cuts in aid programs, all lead to higher debt loads which further hinder accessibility if the student does, in fact, decide to attend a post-secondary education institution.
September 24, 1990

Education involves personal and intellectual development. It gives students a base of skills, as well as cultivating the ability to adapt, innovate and make responsible judgments. In doing so, not only does the student benefit, but society does as well. Individuals return benefits to society by becoming active, working participants in their community. The growing assumption is that for a person to contribute in society, one must have some form of post-secondary education. Without it, Canadians fear they will be left behind.
Although the investment made by the federal government must be considerable, so will be its future return. By making post-secondary education more accessible, more students are given the opportunity to contribute to society upon receiving their qualifications. A post-secondary degree opens the door to better, higher-paying jobs and opportunities. In the long run, support in keeping post-secondary education accessible through lower fees and increased funding, contributes greatly to the economy.
With federal support, education can be an equal base for all students, allowing them to advance according to personal achievement. With decreasing federal support and with fee increases, fewer students will be able to attend a post-secondary education institution. We cannot allow policies that will create a student body composed almost exclusively of those who calculate education simply as an investment in their own future or who can be comfortable with astronomical debts, equivalent to years of employment earnings.
In the past, higher levels of schooling were seen as a factor in economic growth and democracization of the system was seen as a necessary condition for greater social and political equality. Both the federal and provincial governments called education a top priority. The general public rallied to that idea and we saw an increased demand for higher education and an increased demand for extensive financial support from governments. Even today, 88 per cent of Canadians do not want the cuts to post-secondary education that the government has proposed in Bill C-69.
The objectives became to expand and diversify institutions and to encourage individuals to pursue higher education while providing financial assistance to those most in need. To meet the goals, a number of policies were implemented. The number of available places in universities were increased. New universities were founded and the non-university, post-secondary educa-

In the seventies, both levels of government also established student aid programs and post-secondary institutions did their part. More flexible admission policies were implemented, short-term and night courses were developed, and satellite campuses and distance education facilities were set up.
As the seventies gave way to the eighties, funding for post-secondary education gave way to financial retrenchment and constraint. A profile of post-secondary students completed in 1987 revealed that their earlier gains were wiped away and areas that needed improvement never received it.
We had an over-representation of richer Canadians, and an under-representation of those groups who had previously been under-represented: native peoples, women, visible minorities and so on. It also found that students from more modest backgrounds chose a community college education as opposed to university education more often than those in the higher income level.
More people look to education as an alternative as labour markets became more difficult. Many attended post-secondary education institutions for the first time.
Student fees began to be pushed upwards. In the eighties, the percentage of university budgets derived from student fees edged up from 10.6 per cent to 14.5 per cent. Including other costs, students are now responsible for carrying over 25 per cent of university costs. Some call for the deregulation of fees and the privatization of the post-secondary education system. But to do so would ignore the federal responsibility to our children and their future, as well as the future of Canada.
The federal government has an obligation to provide for the national interest and the common good of Canada. This is too great a responsibility to be left solely to the provinces because the long and short-term consequences affect the nation as a whole.
The standard of education throughout Canada must be guaranteed, and it is a shame that this government is perfectly content to cut money to the have not provinces as well as to the have provinces. This decision is leading to a two-tier if not more tiered system, a system which will enable the wealthy to have a better system of education than the less wealthy.

September 24, 1990
Adjournment Debate
This government is not dealing with the education crisis. It is covering up the problem, presumably hoping it will go away. It is doing this without treating the in-depth problem and is disregarding the damage done to Canada's national and cultural consciousness as well as the economic stability of future generations of Canadians.
The government can and must do more. Canadians need and deserve better support for their post-secondary education system. Without it, the future of Canada is at stake. It is time that the government realized that words alone do not solve the problem. Action must speak louder than words.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing makes a number of points that I cannot help but agree with, because he is talking about the people who are the future of Canada.
Of course we all realize that not only those who are attending post-secondary schools in 1990, 1991 or 1992 but for the decades to come will continue to represent the true future of our country.
If we are really going to be looking after their future and the future of this country properly, we have to recognize that the biggest problem we are facing in Canada is the annual deficit.
I am proud to say that this government has addressed expenditures. It has tried to maintain restraint programs more than any other government in Canada in history.
When we first came to office, the federal government was spending $16 billion more on programs than it was collecting in revenues. Today our program spending is $9 billion less than revenues. This is a $25 billion a year turnaround in the stretch of a five-year restraint program.
Seventy per cent of this progress has resulted from expenditure restraint. To achieve that progress, we have reduced program spending as a share of the economy to the lowest level in almost 20 years.
Significant progress has been made in reducing the deficit problem that this government inherited. However, more needs to be done because of the huge deficits built up before 1984.
Federal transfers to the provinces are simply too large for us to ignore. Our transfers to the provinces have been increasing over the last five years at 6.5 per cent annually. Our expenditures have been increasing at only 3.6 per cent. Cash transfers alone to the provinces represent 24 per cent of all of our program spending.
Therefore, in this budget the proposal is to hold the per capita transfers for the next two fiscal years. These transfers have not been cut, they have been capped. It is part of a responsible government's job to ensure that there is a strong, healthy future for young Canadians. [Translation]
